passages.text: The question: How does value belong to a unit as activity in coexistence, and how is it understood, established, and fulfilled in human living? What forms does value take, what endures or changes with time, and in what senses can values be compared? How does the Co-existentialism of Shri A. Nagraj compare with Advaita Vedanta, modern Western value theory, and the natural and social sciences?

This study examines value, evaluation, and the ordering of values in Madhyasth Darshan (Co-existentialism), as presented by Shri A. Nagraj. Its central problem is how value belongs to active units in coexistence and takes different forms in human living. It asks what remains definite through changing circumstances, how those forms are related, and what warrants comparison and correct evaluation.

The Ontology of Coexistence supplies the account of Omnipresence, units, form, properties, essential nature, dharma, the four orders, and jeevan. The Epistemology of Coexistence examines knowing, believing, recognising, fulfilling, and evaluating. Axiology connects that ground and those activities with the forms of mulya: the harmonies of jeevan, humane conduct, relationship values and their expressions, and usefulness, aesthetic qualification, and symbolic valuation in things. Recognition and learning concern how their meanings become understood and reliably fulfilled.

Ethics, aesthetics, prosperity, family relationships, and education develop particular applications of this account. Axiology must nevertheless explain their common basis. It cannot leave labour, material provision, or educational practice outside its argument when fulfilment and evaluation depend on them. The comparison with Advaita, Western philosophy, and science tests both this explanatory reach and the warrant for its claims.

passages.heading: standpoint-and-scope
passages.text: Standpoint and scope

passages.heading: standpoint-and-scope
passages.text: These studies are written from the standpoint of a scientist and technologist — someone trained to graduate-level physics and mathematics, at home with contemporary cosmology, quantum theory, conservation laws, and the logic of formal models.

passages.heading: standpoint-and-scope
passages.text: From that background, value can appear to be something minds add to an otherwise valueless world: a preference, a reward signal, or a social convention. Scientific accounts of mechanism and measurement do not by themselves settle whether this appearance is correct. The status of well-being, the passage from factual description to obligation, and the possibility of goods independent of actual preference remain questions for investigation.

passages.heading: standpoint-and-scope
passages.text: This paper reads the primary Madhyasth Darshan texts, states the account they develop, and compares it with Advaita Vedanta, modern Western philosophy, and the natural and social sciences. Physics and mathematics are one leg of the comparison. The purpose is rigorous comparative understanding through definitions, arguments, textual accuracy, and fit with public knowledge, rather than persuasion or devotional endorsement.

passages.heading: standpoint-and-scope
passages.text: The philosophy is presented in clear, checkable prose. An optional appendix records the structural relations of value through qualitative predicates, distinguishing primary definitions from the assumptions of a formal reconstruction. A fuller mathematical treatment may follow as definitions become stable across the studies; understanding the exposition requires no mathematical formalism.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1. The Madhyasth Darshan Answer

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan holds that value belongs to existence as coexistence. A unit has value through its essentiality and participation, whether anyone approves of it or recognises it correctly. Human beings encounter this value through jeevan, whose activities include recognition, evaluation, and the fulfilment of values in relationships and work. Human living involves several forms of mulya: their content, the circumstances of fulfilment, and the purposes they serve determine what can endure, change, or be compared. Awakening brings these activities into accordance with reality and makes their fulfilment continuous in living.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.1 The active unit and value as essentiality

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Value (mulya) names the essentiality (maulikta) of a unit in coexistence. Essentiality concerns the unit’s characteristic participation and the innateness it bears in its order of existence. It belongs to the unit through its essential nature (swabhav) and dharma, and remains the basis of evaluation whether it is correctly recognised or mistaken (MVD, pp. 47, 124–125; SB, pp. 50, 87).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Entire beingness implies the essentiality of units in every plane and order. Essentiality refers to value.” — SB, p. 50

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: A unit is a definite whole of activity. Form (roop) concerns its bounded configuration; properties (guna) concern its relative powers and their effects in mutuality; essential nature concerns the characteristic conduct and usefulness of those powers in its order; dharma concerns its inseparable innateness. These aspects belong together in the existing unit. A quantitative description establishes dimensions, amounts, or rates; understanding essentiality identifies what the activity amounts to in participation, such as integration, nourishment, protection, or resolution. This qualitative significance is the subject of value (MVD, p. 47; SB, pp. 60–62, 87; AVD, p. 184).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The unit’s activeness is grounded in its saturation in Omnipresence, satta: the all-pervading ground in which units exist and remain active. The Ontology of Coexistence, §1.2, develops saturation and effort–motion–result; here they ground value in the unit’s continuing activity. Strength (bal) in state (sthiti) and power (shakti) in motion (gati) are inseparable aspects of its activity. Basic impulsion (mool cheshta) is expressed through effort, motion, and result (shram–gati–parinam): effort is aligned with dharma and essential nature, motion with essential nature and properties, and result with form. Essential nature thus participates in both the strength borne and the power expressed. These relations describe the same continuing activity in mutuality (MVD, pp. 35, 40; SB, pp. 60–62).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The four orders differ in their characteristic participation. The material order manifests integration and disintegration; the pranic order adds growth and vitalising or devitalising conduct. Animal living joins body and jeevan, with the hope to live; the knowledge order brings the human possibility of understanding and the purpose of happiness. Formation and dissolution both participate in natural orderliness. The significance of an effect must therefore be understood through the order and mutuality involved. Reciprocal participation in insentient units and reflective human evaluation have their respective places in this account (SB, pp. 179–182, 249).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Human essential nature is expressed in the human values of fortitude, courage, generosity, kindness, grace, and compassion; human dharma is happiness. Human beings fulfil their value through orderliness in themselves and participation in wider orderliness. Knowing concerns understanding reality, while believing concerns accepting a meaning as a basis of activity; correct recognition depends on their accord (The Epistemology of Coexistence, §1.5). Human conduct can be inhumane, humane, or higher-humane as understanding develops, while happiness remains human dharma through both mistaken and resolved attempts to attain it (MVD, pp. 15, 97, 115, 125; SB, pp. 179–182, 249).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Essentiality is already present in the active unit. Human understanding can become established, and labour can establish a useful configuration of material. The former concerns the knower’s acceptance and conduct; the latter concerns what the configured material can fulfil. Both take place within an existence whose units already have essentiality (MVD, pp. 56, 83, 124–125; SB, p. 87).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.2 The structure of value in jeevan

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Jeevan is the conscious unit whose faculties are atma, buddhi, chitta, vritti, and mun. The harmonies of these faculties are one form of value among those distinguished in §1.3. Values inherent in jeevan are activities: they are understood, accepted, felt, evaluated, and expressed through its living. Usefulness, also called object value, belongs to things; human experience and evaluation of value belong to jeevan. Evaluation itself is sentiment activity, bhav-kriya, whose correctness depends on awakening (MVD, p. 203; JV, pp. 137–139).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Actionless, changeless knowledge is named chetana in relation to sentient nature, chaitanya; The Epistemology of Coexistence, §1.1, develops this distinction. Realisation and the understanding of value belong to the activity of jeevan saturated in that ground (MVD, pp. 35, 74–75, 97–100; SB, pp. 63–64).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The relation of state and motion gives value an active structure within each faculty. State is the strength borne in the activity; motion is its expression as power. In awakened jeevan, the understood basis and its meaningful expression have the following forms (KD, §3.8, p. 84).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Faculty Activity in state / strength Activity in motion / power Atma Realisation (anubhav) Evidence (praman) Buddhi Understanding (bodh) of actuality, reality, and truth Resolve (sankalp) to express it Chitta Contemplation (chintan), with direct apprehension (sakshatkar) of justice, dharma, and truth Visualisation (chitran) Vritti Deliberation or comparison (tulan) in justice, dharma, and truth Analysis (vishleshan) Mun Tasting (asvadan) the value accepted Selection (chayan) for its meaningful fulfilment

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The faculties also bear definite relations to one another. Happiness (sukh), peace (shanti), contentment (santosh), and bliss (anand) name harmonies between their activities. Concurrence (samatva) or absence of opposition (nirvirodh) has a specified content: happiness is resolution with behaviour free of wrongdoing; peace involves thought free of injustice; contentment involves desire free of attachment; bliss involves understanding free of ignorance. The value is the harmony lived and felt in those activities (MVD, pp. 327–328, 331, 333, 346; JV, p. 138; MAD, reader p. 47).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Jeevan value Harmony between faculties Cumulative fulfilment in living Happiness (sukh) Mun and vritti Resolution Peace (shanti) Vritti and chitta Resolution and prosperity Contentment (santosh) Chitta and buddhi Resolution, prosperity, and fearlessness Bliss (anand) Buddhi and atma Resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The cumulative fulfilment connects these harmonies with human living: each wider fulfilment retains the preceding content (KD, §3.12, p. 112). These fulfilments extend from the person through family and society to universal orderliness, as developed in The Ontology of Coexistence, §1.15. Inner satisfaction becomes evident through self-governed conduct across these relationships (JV, pp. 53, 62, 140; AVD, p. 228). The harmonies’ structural definiteness lies in the specified relations of activity and their understood meaning. A person’s actual understanding and conduct determine whether the harmony is fulfilled; self-examination and evidence in living bear on whether its presence has been correctly recognised (§1.4; §§A.1–A.3).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Contentment includes freedom from the sentiment of lack together with readiness to evidence production beyond need through science aligned with wisdom. Its paired expression is abundance, shree. Bliss is borne at buddhi; ultimate bliss, paramanand, belongs to realisation in atma, with authenticity as its expression and evidence. The concurrence of atma and Omnipresence is eternally present, while realisation brings that reality into awakened human living (MVD, pp. 327–328, 331; JV, p. 138).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Evaluation at vritti can take pleasant–unpleasant, beneficial–harmful, and gain–loss as its perspectives. These orient attention towards sensory attraction, bodily advantage, and acquisition. The humane perspectives are justice–injustice, dharma–adharma, and truth–untruth. Justice concerns fulfilled values in relationships; human dharma concerns resolution and happiness; truth concerns coexistence as it is. Under humane understanding, pleasure and bodily health have their place within justice, while prosperity replaces acquisitive profit as the economic purpose (MVD, pp. 58, 66, 336–337; JV, pp. 139–140).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Correct evaluation involves the coordinated activity of the whole jeevan. Contemplation and direct apprehension at chitta concern the reality whose meaning is visualised; understanding at buddhi supplies certainty and resolve; realisation at atma grounds its evidence in living. Deliberation, analysis, tasting, and selection express that understood meaning. A person can visualise a desirable result and calculate how to obtain it while still misunderstanding the relationship involved. Establishment of understanding concerns the development through which these activities accord with reality and become continuous in fulfilment (MVD, pp. 83, 99–100, 156, 203; KD, p. 84).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Constitutional completeness is jeevan’s settled constitution, activity completeness its freedom from delusion, and conduct completeness the continuity of that understanding in living; The Ontology of Coexistence, §§1.6–1.6.3, develops these transitions, distinguishing inherent capacity from its fulfilment in understanding and conduct (MVD, p. 83; KD, p. 37).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3 Forms of value in human living

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The principal forms of value bring different aspects of human living into view: the harmonies of jeevan, humane essential nature, established relationship values and their expressions, and usefulness and aesthetic value in things. Symbolic value concerns money and assigned valuation in exchange (MVD, pp. 183, 306; JV, pp. 43, 55, 137–139). Their bearers, fulfilment, and relations can be distinguished as follows.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Form of value Bearer and meaning Time Kind of comparison Jeevan values Happiness, peace, contentment, and bliss as faculty harmonies Enduring content; fulfilment concerns present activity Cumulative fulfilment (§1.2) Human values Human essential nature in conduct Enduring content; conduct develops Humane and higher-humane expression Established values Values borne in sthiti/bal and fulfilled in relationships Relational content endures across time and place Trust as common; love as complete Expressed or civic values Corresponding outward values in gati/shakti Acts and means meet changing circumstances Each expression is dedicated to its established counterpart Usefulness value What a thing can fulfil in nourishment, protection, and participation Constancy and temporality claims distinguished in §1.5 Greater or less for a specified need; assessed apart from price Aesthetic value Convenience and aesthetic qualification added to usefulness Temporal with usefulness (§1.5) Added convenience assessed relative to usefulness Symbolic value Money and assigned monetary valuation Amount or price can change Monetary amounts; usefulness assessed separately

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: These forms participate together in living. Generosity, for example, articulates humane essential nature and also gives expression to care in a relationship. The faculty location of a relationship value identifies a named activity within the coordinated jeevan. Its understanding and fulfilment involve the meaning of the relationship and the whole conscious unit (MVD, pp. 125, 203, 331–340; AVD, pp. 91–94). The temporal claims about usefulness are stated separately in §1.5 and examined in §7.5; enduring relational content and situated fulfilment are developed in §1.4 (MAD, reader p. 51).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Human values articulate the essential nature appropriate to resolved living. Fortitude (dhirata) is firmness towards justice; courage (veerta) deploys intellectual and physical powers to make justice available; generosity (udarta) offers body, mind, and wealth according to need for awakening, health, and prosperity. These characterise humane expression. Kindness (daya), grace (kripa), and compassion (karuna) characterise higher-humane expression: kindness supplies missing content where receptivity is present, grace develops missing receptivity where content is available, and compassion works to make both available where both are absent. Love includes their combined expression (MVD, pp. 52, 60–61, 125, 331, 340).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Established values (sthapit mulya) are borne in strength or state; expressed values, also called civic or shishta values, are their corresponding expressions in motion or power. Their one-to-one correspondence gives understood value a definite form of expression. The nine principal established relationship values and their expressions occupy the following named positions (MAD, reader p. 30; JV, p. 108; AVD, pp. 91–94; MVD, pp. 331–340).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Established value in bal / sthiti Corresponding expressed value in gati Faculty Care (mamta) Generosity (udarta) Mun Guidance (vatsalya) Naturalness (sahajta) Chitta Trust (vishwas) Concordance (saujanyata) Vritti Affection (sneha) Dedication (nishtha) Mun Gratitude (kritagyata) Humility (saumyata) Vritti Glory (gaurav) Simplicity (saralta) Vritti Love (prem) Non-otherness (ananyata) Chitta Reverence (shraddha) Devoutness (pujyata) Chitta Respect (samman) Cordiality (sauhardta) Mun

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Care sustains nurture and protection; guidance sustains development towards comprehensive understanding. Affection gives continuity to just meeting; gratitude acknowledges help received towards development; glory accepts an example for emulation; reverence moves towards excellence and completeness; respect accepts excellence in personality and talent. Their expressions make these acceptances evident in conduct (MVD, pp. 331–340).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Trust joins fulfilled mutual value with understanding of orderliness and communication of resolution. Its expression is cooperation, participation, and complementarity. Love includes realisation of completeness and the combined expression of kindness, grace, and compassion; non-otherness expresses it through complementary activity with human beings and the rest of nature. Trust is the common relationship value (samya mulya), and love the complete value (purna mulya) (MVD, pp. 331, 336; MAD, reader pp. 30, 43).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.4 Recognition, establishment, fulfilment and justice

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: A relationship (sambandh) is a mutuality whose expectations are predetermined towards completeness. A contact (sampark) is a mutuality whose expectations are voluntarily determined. Both involve value and are answerable to justice. Agreed expectations carry responsibilities concerning what is undertaken and how it is fulfilled (MVD, pp. 61–62; KD, p. 20).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Established relationship values endure across proximity and distance, past, present, and future. Their definite content supplies the basis for recognising what is due. The intellectual and material means of fulfilment are assessed in the circumstances: nurturing a child or helping a learner calls for suitable resources, ability, and receptivity. Care can remain the recognised value while the food, protection, or help required changes with the person’s situation (MAD, reader p. 51; MVD, pp. 61–62, 331–340).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The actual relationship and the person’s recognition of it can differ. Knowing and believing concern correctness of recognition; fulfilment gives recognised value expression in mutuality. When the meaning of a relationship is understood and accepted, its value becomes available as the basis of selection and participation. In this sense understanding becomes established in the person, and the corresponding expression becomes available for continuing fulfilment. The value’s essential content remains the reference through these changes in understanding and conduct (MVD, pp. 83, 97, 203; JV, pp. 138–139; KD, p. 84).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The named relationships include parent–child, sibling, spousal, master–associate, teacher–student, friendship, and orderliness relationships. Family Relationships and Values, §§1.1.3–1.2.1, develops these names through the responsibilities and purposes they identify. Their fulfilment involves comprehensive resolution, nurturing, protection, usefulness or complementarity, right-use, and purposeful-use. Humane duty consists in acts that fulfil values; family, society, and orderliness also confer rights within participation (MVD, pp. 61–62, 190; JV, pp. 108–109).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Justice comprises recognition of relationships, fulfilment of their values, evaluation, and mutual satisfaction. Evaluation examines whether participation has fulfilled the recognised responsibility and whether the outcome accords with human essentiality. The relationship and its values supply the standard; mutual satisfaction is the fulfilment of this relational process (MVD, pp. 311, 336).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Evaluation also guides deliberation before action. The person recognises the responsibility, assesses available means, and selects an appropriate contribution. Accomplished participation then supplies the outcome to evaluate. Self-examination asks whether justice is present on both sides; the resulting conduct and its effects also become evident to those with whom the person lives and works (JV, pp. 98, 138–139; KD, p. 84).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Nourishing a child illustrates these distinctions. The food’s usefulness concerns what it can provide for nourishment. Care concerns the recognised relationship and responsibility for nurture, while generosity expresses the offering of available means. The caregiver’s understanding, the adequacy of the food and provision, and the child’s actual nourishment enter the assessment in their respective ways. The example brings object usefulness, human understanding, and relational fulfilment into one participation (§§1.3, 1.5).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Understanding the responsibility can coexist with inadequate resources or skill. An effective contribution can also occur while a learner is still developing the understanding that would make it independently sustained. Claims to established care therefore call for examination of both understood meaning and responsibilities actually fulfilled. This distinction gives education a practical task: develop correct recognition, capacity and means, and continuity of fulfilment (§1.8; MVD, pp. 61, 94, 203).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The same jeevan recognises, evaluates, and tastes value. Happiness, peace, contentment, and bliss are present in the experience of established values; inward harmony and outward fulfilment belong together in meaningful participation (JV, pp. 138–139; MAD, reader p. 51). What has been expressed can be examined again in thought and settled in understanding. Further expression can then embody a clarified recognition, a corrected means, or an understanding sustained through its evidence (MVD, pp. 83, 218; KD, pp. 112–113).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.5 The value of things

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Usefulness value (upyogita mulya) concerns what a thing can do for nourishment, bodily protection, and participation. Food, housing, and adornment figure among common aspirations, with transport and communication among special aspirations. Understanding human purposes and family needs guides the assessment of what should be produced, acquired, and used (MVD, pp. 56–57; JV, p. 123).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Usefulness is described as definite through examples of useful things. A kilogram of wheat is said to have the same usefulness as a hundred years earlier, with interference nevertheless capable of diminishing it. The usefulness of sesame, medicine, rice, wheat, and vegetables is likewise described as constant. Aesthetic addition is meaningful where convenience is added to usefulness (JV, pp. 123, 137–138).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Usefulness and beauty are also described as temporal (samayik), because needs, use, exchange, and deployment are temporal. This account identifies enduring established, human, and jeevan values as the basis of stable social living (MAD, reader p. 51). The relation between this temporal description and the constancy claims remains a textual question (§7.5).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Human labour can establish usefulness and aesthetic value on natural abundance. Application (prayog) is the endeavour, continued until success, to establish these values through labour in response to need; production (utpadan) standardises the successful process. Here establishment concerns a useful configuration and its capacity for fulfilment. Production–work includes the skills, resources, agriculture, and industry through which families can produce beyond assessed need (MVD, pp. 56, 260, 268; JV, pp. 137–138).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Money is symbolic value (prateek mulya). An increase in its quantity or in the price assigned to a good does not itself increase the good’s usefulness. Manufactured scarcity can raise symbolic valuation while obstructing access to things people need. Prosperity consequently requires understanding need, the ability and readiness to produce adequate provision, and its availability for right-use (MVD, pp. 183, 331; SB, pp. 211–212).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Use deploys means in production and service. Right-use (sadupyog) directs body, mind, and wealth towards participation in family orderliness. Purposeful-use (prayojansheelta) serves awakening, undivided society, and universal orderliness. These ends give purposeful-use a social scope from family to world society (How Undivided Society Is Established, §1.1; MVD, p. 57).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In nourishing a child, the food’s preparation gives useful material an appropriate form, while its provision fulfils a responsibility of care. Price records a monetary valuation; nourishment and fulfilled care require their own assessment (§1.4).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Exchange requires evaluation of labour and of the goods through which its results become available. The proposed order protects labour and its fruits from exploitation and seeks exchange of labour-valued goods free from profit and loss. Labour deployment belongs to production; labour-value assessment belongs to exchange; evaluation of established and expressed values belongs to justice. These are distinct responsibilities within the same social order (MVD, pp. 260, 268–269; SB, p. 237).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Rightful wealth can be received through remuneration, gift, and award. Material provision thus includes legitimate receiving alongside production, with implications for the care of people whose needs exceed their present productive capacity (AVD, p. 170; MVD, pp. 61, 340). Production and use also involve the other orders: natural abundance is to be used in accordance with usefulness and regeneration, and human participation is to nurture the conditions of coexistence (SB, pp. 141, 200–201). The ecological decisions and procedures needed to fulfil that responsibility remain questions for investigation (§7.9).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.6 How values are ordered

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The forms of value are related through dedication (samarpan). Usefulness serves need; need serves expressed or shishta value; expressed value serves established value; established value serves human value; and human value serves jeevan value. This order gives production and material provision their purpose in fulfilled relationships, humane conduct, and the harmony of jeevan. Need links useful means with the values their deployment fulfils (MAD, reader p. 34).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Higher value (guru mulyan) concerns a long-lasting result or non-transformability. Advancement moves towards higher value or resolution, and mutual ascent supports such development. The contrast with lower value and decline concerns the endurance and direction of fulfilment. This supplies a criterion of development through which greater or lesser value can be considered (MVD, pp. 43, 110, 126).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Inclusion has its own scope. The account of the four orders describes the more developed as including what is borne in the less developed: the higher order retains the properties, essential nature, and dharma of the lower orders within its more comprehensive living. The relation is asymmetric; the less comprehensive cannot encompass the more comprehensive within its existing measure. Knowing the more developed remains possible and belongs to the opportunity for development (MVD, pp. 47, 219–222; KD, p. 37). Cumulative fulfilment in human living likewise retains resolution as prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence become fulfilled (§1.2; KD, p. 112).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Commonness and completeness concern the scope of relationship value. Trust is common in relationships, while love is complete in its encompassing participation and expression of kindness, grace, and compassion. These determinations concern what is fulfilled in mutuality (MAD, reader pp. 30, 43).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Dedication therefore specifies the purpose served, endurance concerns lasting fulfilment, inclusion concerns the content retained in more comprehensive development, and commonness or completeness concerns the scope of relationship value. Each relation makes a particular kind of comparison intelligible. Their implications for contested obligations and allocation require examination in the actual relationships involved (§§7.1, 7.7).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Acquisitive profit gives greater and lesser worth a different purpose: obtaining greater worth in return for lesser worth or labour. The other party may surrender the greater through helplessness, willingness, or ignorance. This perspective is rejected in favour of prosperity through production and exchange governed by justice. Pleasure and bodily health remain within humane living, while useful provision serves resolved relationships and the fulfilment of jeevan (MVD, pp. 58, 67; JV, pp. 139–140).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.7 Error and awakening

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Delusion involves over-evaluation, under-evaluation, and mis-evaluation. Something may be assigned a significance greater or smaller than its essentiality warrants, or recognised as something other than what it is (MVD, pp. 152, 306). Mistaking a rope for a snake illustrates mis-evaluation; mistaking iron for gold or gold for iron illustrates over- and under-evaluation (SB, PDF p. 146). At the human level these errors affect self-assessment, relationships, acquisition, and the use of resources.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Correct evaluation develops with awakening. Nirakarshan, freedom from attraction or attachment in the relevant definition, is freedom from the three evaluative errors. It permits conduct governed by essentiality. Non-doership concerns freedom from wrongful action within a life that remains active. Self-evaluation is the first step in the study of awakening, and complete correctness belongs to the coordinated activity of awakened jeevan (MVD, pp. 87, 152, 203).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Fear and temptation direct relationships through threatened harm or promised acquisition. They cannot serve as relationship values or be evaluated as fulfilled values. Recognition of relationships, their responsibilities, and mutual satisfaction provides the humane basis of participation (JV, pp. 109–110).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Human beings deploy body, mind, and wealth towards what they regard as most valuable. Under delusion the four basic instincts—eating, sleep, defence, and mating—are treated as the highest purpose; discerning evaluation can place the three eshanas—progeny, wealth, and reputation—highest; delusionless evaluation places freedom from delusion highest. Evaluation in these states is correspondingly named attachment, awakening, and reality. The change concerns the evaluator’s understanding and the purpose directing desire and conduct (MVD, pp. 58, 60, 319).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The body serves nourishment, protection, and participation; jeevan fulfils its purpose through understanding and happiness. Awakening develops the recognition of these purposes and their proper relation. The evaluator can then recognise usefulness, relational responsibility, and inward fulfilment in their respective places (JV, pp. 93–94, 123).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.8 Continuity of value in persons and tradition

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Continuity concerns understood value becoming a sustained basis of fulfilment. A person can act generously on one occasion and later respond with miserliness. The earlier contribution may have fulfilled a need, while generosity has yet to become continuous. Establishment involves the person’s own understanding, through which meaningful conduct can be sustained across circumstances (MVD, pp. 61, 94; KD, pp. 37, 84).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Sanskar comprises acceptances towards completeness and the understanding and tendencies through which meaningful activity is expressed. It includes bodily, verbal, and mental participation through doing, enabling another’s doing, and consenting. Susanskar supports awakening and resolved living; kusanskar supports decline. What a person understands and accepts thus bears on subsequent conduct and on the examples made available to others (MVD, pp. 90, 94).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Learning from another’s conduct can occasion rethinking. Aapyayan, internal reception, concerns welcoming, tasting, and taking value into oneself, evidenced through evaluation. Parimarjan, qualitative refinement, concerns change in hope, thought, desire, and resolve. What is expressed and examined in living can become accepted in understanding and realisation and supply the basis for further expression. These activities connect received example, the learner’s own understanding, and continuing participation (MAD, reader p. 45; MVD, pp. 94, 99–100; KD, pp. 112–113).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Understood value is evidenced in lawful work, just relationships, resolution, and realised coexistence (MVD, pp. 12, 80, 174); The Ontology of Coexistence, §1.11, develops law and conformance. Education, justice, production, exchange, and health are institutional fields for examining fulfilment, developed in its §1.15 (MVD, p. 260; AVD, p. 265). Values supply purposes whose continuing determinations in wealth, behaviour, and use of means belong to character and ethics (JV, p. 55; Ethics and Morals in Human Beings, §§3.1, 3.5–3.6).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Education develops knowing, believing, recognising, and fulfilling through study, practice, and self-evaluation (KD, pp. 18–19; MVD, p. 87); The Epistemology of Coexistence, §§1.5–1.6, examines these activities and their transmission.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Understood meaning, actual fulfilment, and evidence of fulfilment remain distinguishable. Appendix A states their structural relations; §7.8 examines how learning becomes establishment and continuity.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2. The Advaita Vedanta Answer

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita Vedanta relates the dearness of persons and goods to the Self, Atman, whose identity with Brahman is known in liberation. Human purposes include material provision, enjoyment, and right conduct, while liberation concerns freedom from the ignorance through which finite attainments are sought as ultimate fulfilment. Value is consequently examined through dearness, the ends of life, and discrimination between enduring reality and changing goods (BU, 2.4.5 with Shankara’s commentary; BSB, 1.1.1, 1.1.4).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.1 The Self, dearness and fullness

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: “It is not for the sake of all, my dear, that all is loved, but for one’s own sake that it is loved. The Self, my dear Maitreyī, should be realised…” — BU, 2.4.5

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The Self is primary in dearness; husband, wife, children, and wealth are dear for its sake. Inquiry into this dearness leads beyond the limited individual with whom one ordinarily identifies to knowledge of the Self (BU, 2.4.5 with Shankara’s commentary).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The Upanishadic teaching identifies Brahman as truth, knowledge, and infinity (satyam jnanam anantam), and as the source of joy. Advaita’s later compact formulation—being, consciousness, and bliss, sat-cit-ananda—brings these descriptions together as names of its undivided nature. Finite pleasures depend on conditions and degrees of freedom from desire; Brahman’s bliss is its own nature, disclosed through knowledge (TU, 2.1.1, 2.7–2.9 with Shankara’s commentary). The Ontology of Coexistence, §2.2, develops these descriptions of Brahman.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The dearness of a person, the nourishment provided by food, and the security sought through wealth have their place in empirical life. Their finite satisfactions lead the inquiry towards the Self as the ground of fulfilment. Ethical duties govern how such goods are pursued and how others are treated (BU, 2.4.5; BG, 3.8, 16.1–16.3).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.2 Human purposes and empirical virtues

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The four purusharthas distinguish purposes of human life: dharma, right living and duty; artha, material means; kama, enjoyment; and moksha, liberation. Advaita distinguishes pursuit of the first three with attachment to their fruits from the inquiry into liberation as the highest human purpose (BG, 18.34; BSB, 1.1.1). Acquisition and enjoyment remain answerable to dharma: desire compatible with duty includes bodily maintenance, while accumulation through unjust means is condemned (BG, 7.11, 16.12 with Shankara’s commentary).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Within empirical living, vyavahara, duties and virtues guide action. Fearlessness, purity of mind, generosity, self-control, truthfulness, compassion, and freedom from anger are qualities of conduct that orient the person towards liberation (BG, 16.1–16.3). Discrimination of the enduring from the transient, nitya/anitya, concerns the reality and persistence of what is sought. Purposes, virtues, and this discrimination thus address different aspects of evaluation (BSB, 1.1.1; VC, vv. 17–20).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.3 Superimposition and mistaken valuation

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Ignorance involves adhyasa, mutual superimposition of Self and not-Self. Bodily and mental conditions are attributed to the Self, while the consciousness and selfhood of the Self are attributed to body and mind. The resulting identification sustains the experience of being a limited agent and enjoyer (BSB, Introduction). Its evaluative consequence is that changes in possessions, sensations, or standing can be taken to secure or diminish one’s very fulfilment. Dwelling on objects develops attachment, desire, and, when frustrated, anger and loss of discrimination (BG, 2.62–2.63).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Correction therefore requires inquiry into what the Self is, alongside restraint of attachment in conduct. Ordinary knowledge can correct an error about an object; liberating knowledge removes the identification that gives finite acquisition its promise of ultimate completion (BSB, 1.1.4). The Epistemology of Coexistence, §2.3, develops superimposition, correction, and the distinction between empirical and ultimate reality.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.4 Enduring fulfilment and the ordering of purposes

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Acquired goods and pleasurable experiences arise under conditions and can cease. Liberation is unproduced: knowledge discloses the Self’s freedom rather than making it a new result of action. Its priority concerns enduring freedom from ignorance and dependence on further acquisition. The distinction between nitya and anitya directs aspiration towards this fulfilment (BSB, 1.1.1, 1.1.4; VC, vv. 17–20).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The ordering has two connected relations: dharma governs the pursuit of finite goods, while liberation directs the inquiry into ultimate fulfilment. Material support and disciplined action can prepare a person for knowledge (BG, 3.8, 3.19, 7.11, 16.12; BSB, 1.1.1). Their usefulness in preparation differs from the freedom knowledge discloses. The practical implications of this ordering for comparison and allocation are examined in §5.6.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.5 Useful things, action and attachment

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Objects have empirical use: bodily maintenance requires action and provision, and engagement with necessary sensory objects can proceed with restraint, free from attraction and aversion (BG, 2.64, 3.8 with Shankara’s commentary). Attachment concerns the identification and craving through which their acquisition or loss governs the person (BSB, 1.1.4). At the ultimate standpoint, paramartha, objects have no reality independent of Brahman; empirical usefulness belongs to the domain in which needs, actions, and their consequences occur (BSB, 2.1.13–2.1.14).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Action without attachment supports purification and knowledge. Loka-sangraha, the holding together of the world, also gives action a social purpose: the wise must consider the effect of their example on those engaged in action. Such activity can continue without the realised person’s identification as an individual doer (BG, 3.19–3.20, 3.25–3.26 with Shankara’s commentary). Goods and work consequently have practical and ethical significance, while liberation remains distinct from anything their production can accomplish.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.6 Knowledge, evidence and responsibility

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Knowledge of the Self proceeds through scriptural teaching, shruti, hearing, reflection, and contemplation. Discrimination, dispassion, restraint, and concentration qualify the inquirer (BU, 2.4.5; BSB, 1.1.1). The decisive issue is the removal of mistaken identification: pleasure and material success cannot by themselves establish knowledge of the Self (BSB, 1.1.4).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Evaluation thus asks both whether finite goods serve legitimate empirical purposes and whether the fulfilment sought through them rests on a correct understanding of the Self. Compassion and concern for one’s effect on others have continuing significance in empirical conduct, including the example offered by the wise (BG, 3.25–3.26, 16.1–16.3). Empirical duty is assessed within vyavahara, while liberating knowledge concerns the Self’s already free nature (BSB, 1.1.4).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: 3. Modern Western Philosophy on Value

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Modern Western value theory contains competing accounts of what is good, what bears value, and how value is known. The discussion moves from grounds and warranted judgment to well-being, value ordering, economic goods, and relationships. Metaethics examines the status of normative judgments; welfare theory examines what makes life go well for a person; practical philosophy examines reasons, duties, and conflicts. These inquiries overlap without yielding a single Western doctrine (SEP Value Theory).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: 3.1 Intrinsic, final and instrumental value

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Something can be valued as a means to another good or for its own sake. This final–instrumental distinction differs from the distinction between value grounded in intrinsic features and value dependent on relations or context. A historically significant object, for example, may be valued for its own sake partly because of its history (SEP Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Value).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Moore asks what would be good considered in isolation, but also argues that the value of a whole need not equal the sum of its parts’ values. His principle of organic unities makes the configuration of a valuable whole matter to assessment. Intrinsic value therefore does not invariably entail simple addition of separately valued constituents (Moore 1903, §§18–22).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: 3.2 Natural facts and normative conclusions

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Hume calls attention to the unexplained transition from statements about what is to conclusions about what ought to be. Moore’s open-question argument challenges proposed definitions of goodness in terms of some other property: understanding that something has the property appears to leave open whether it is good (Hume 1739, III.1.1; Moore 1903, §§10–14).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: The two arguments address different problems. Hume’s passage concerns inference; Moore’s concerns the analysis of goodness. Neither by itself settles every form of ethical naturalism. A theory may propose a substantive rather than definitional identity, or argue for normative standards through the characteristic flourishing of living beings. Such proposals require arguments for the identification and for its practical authority (SEP Natural Law Ethics; SEP Moral Realism).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: 3.3 Realism, construction and anti-realism

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Moral realists hold that some moral judgments are true and that their truth is not exhausted by the speaker’s approval. Naturalist and non-naturalist versions disagree about the relation between moral facts and the natural world. Expressivists explain moral language through practical attitudes and commitments; error theorists argue that ordinary moral claims systematically fail in what they purport to assert (SEP Moral Realism; SEP Moral Anti-Realism).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Constructivist approaches connect normative standards with an appropriate procedure of practical reasoning. Their relation to realism depends on the particular account of construction and objectivity. Expressivist theories likewise develop accounts of disagreement, consistency, and practical criticism. The categories identify research programmes whose adequacy turns on their detailed treatment of truth, reasons, and judgment (SEP Moral Anti-Realism).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: 3.4 Fitting attitudes and reasons

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Fitting-attitude accounts analyse value through the attitudes it is appropriate to have towards an object: admiration, love, desire, or respect, for example. The relevant attitude is fitting, rather than merely actual or widely shared. A central difficulty is distinguishing reasons that bear on an object’s value from incentives or threats that make an attitude advantageous to its holder (SEP Fitting Attitude Theories).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Scanlon’s buck-passing account explains the value of something through other properties that give reasons for appropriate responses. Value identifies the presence of such reasons rather than supplying an additional independent reason. The account shifts inquiry towards what makes a response warranted (Scanlon 1998, ch. 2).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: 3.5 Pleasure, desire and objective goods

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Hedonistic theories make pleasure and the absence of pain central to welfare. Desire theories locate welfare in the fulfilment of desires, often with qualifications concerning information, rationality, or the scope of the person’s concern. Objective-list theories hold that some things can benefit a person independently of current desire or pleasure, such as knowledge, achievement, or worthwhile relationships (Parfit 1984, Appendix I; SEP Well-Being). On virtue accounts grounded in flourishing, good character and its exercise partly constitute living well (SEP Well-Being).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Nozick’s experience machine asks whether an entirely satisfying simulated experience would supply everything that matters in life. The thought experiment tests whether doing things, being a certain person, and contact with reality matter beyond experience. Its force depends on reflection about the case and the intuitions it elicits (Nozick 1974, pp. 42–45).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: 3.6 Plurality, comparison and trade-offs

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Value pluralism holds that more than one irreducible kind of value matters. It need not imply that every pair of options is incomparable. Ranking, comparison through a common measure, compensation for a loss, and practical permission to make a trade-off are distinct questions. Some accounts allow comparison without a common numerical unit; others identify cases where familiar comparative relations fail (Berlin 1969; Raz 1986; Chang 1997; SEP Value Pluralism; SEP Incommensurable Values).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Kant distinguishes price, which permits an equivalent, from dignity, which admits no equivalent. Anderson examines how different goods call for different modes of valuation and how market valuation can be inappropriate in some relations. These positions concern the standards governing valuation and exchange, including cases in which willingness to pay does not decide what should be done (Kant 1785, Section II; Anderson 1993).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Questions of beauty, taste, and the validity of aesthetic judgment are developed in Aesthetics, §2.2.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: 3.7 Scheler and Hartmann on ordered values

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Scheler treats value as objective and disclosed through intentional feeling, with a hierarchy of agreeable, vital, spiritual, and holy values. This feeling is directed towards value rather than being identical with bodily sensation. His account includes distorted valuation and the transformation of attention through love and openness. Hartmann also develops a differentiated order of values and distinguishes the height of a value from the strength of its demand. Ordered value consequently raises questions both of recognition and of what takes priority in action (Scheler 1913–16; Hartmann 1932; SEP Scheler).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: 3.8 Economic value and human development

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Marx distinguishes use-value, the usefulness of a thing, from value in commodity production and its expression in exchange-value. Concrete useful labour produces particular use-values; abstract human labour supplies the account of commodity value, whose magnitude depends on socially necessary labour time. Nature contributes to material wealth, and some useful things have no value in this specific commodity sense. These distinctions prevent a simple identification of usefulness, labour expended by an individual, and exchange price (Marx 1867, ch. 1).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Marginal analysis examines the significance of an additional unit within particular conditions of choice. A thing’s physical capacity alone does not determine its marginal benefit or exchange conditions. The capability approach further distinguishes resources and reported satisfaction from people’s real opportunities to live and act. Sen and Nussbaum make this distinction central to evaluating development, while differing in how capabilities should be specified (Sen 1999; Nussbaum 2011; SEP Capability Approach).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: 3.9 Care, recognition and trust

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Care ethics examines dependence, attentiveness, responsiveness, and the concrete relationship between one who cares and one who receives care. Recognition theory examines the social relations through which practical identity and self-realisation are sustained. These approaches bring the conditions of human development into the account of value; a requirement for social recognition need not make a person’s basic worth depend on whether others currently recognise it (Noddings 1984; Honneth 1995; SEP Recognition).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: Philosophical accounts of trust examine dependence under vulnerability, expectations of another, and the distinction between reliance and trustworthiness. They ask when trust is reasonable and what betrayal damages. Trust is therefore a normative relationship whose success cannot be identified simply with confidence or successful prediction (SEP Trust).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: 3.10 The range of the inquiry

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-on-value
passages.text: These approaches offer different resources for explaining value’s bearers, grounds, recognition, and practical force. A claim about the status of moral truth does not alone determine a theory of welfare; a theory of welfare does not alone determine just distribution. Western value theory makes these distinctions explicit and investigates how they can be joined (SEP Value Theory; SEP Well-Being).

passages.heading: 4-the-natural-and-social-sciences-on-valuation
passages.section: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation
passages.text: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation

passages.heading: 4-the-natural-and-social-sciences-on-valuation
passages.section: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation
passages.text: The natural and social sciences investigate valuation through mechanisms of learning and choice, reports of experience and expectation, and individual and aggregate outcomes such as cooperation, production, and well-being. These objects of inquiry require different measures and explanations. Empirical findings can inform practical judgment about provision, education, relationships, and institutions when joined to an account of which outcomes matter and why. Their evidential strength depends on the design, population, measures, and causal assumptions of each investigation. The studies reviewed here supply neither the darshan’s classes of mulya nor a usefulness-constancy doctrine or a measure of established relationship value.

passages.heading: 4-the-natural-and-social-sciences-on-valuation
passages.section: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation
passages.text: 4.1 Neural valuation and learning

passages.heading: 4-the-natural-and-social-sciences-on-valuation
passages.section: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation
passages.text: Neuroscience distinguishes representing options, learning from outcomes, and selecting actions. Research on value-based choice identifies neural systems through which different options can be compared for a decision. Dopamine reward-prediction-error research concerns differences between expected and received reward and their role in updating expectations (Rangel, Camerer, and Montague 2008; Schultz 2016).

passages.heading: 4-the-natural-and-social-sciences-on-valuation
passages.section: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation
passages.text: The comparison of options and the learning signals that revise expectations perform different functions. A shared neural scale within a task concerns how a decision is implemented. Moral decisions recruit interacting systems whose contributions depend on the task (Crockett 2013).

passages.heading: 4-the-natural-and-social-sciences-on-valuation
passages.section: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation
passages.text: 4.2 Cooperation and moral regularities

passages.heading: 4-the-natural-and-social-sciences-on-valuation
passages.section: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation
passages.text: Evolutionary explanations investigate how cooperation can develop through processes such as repeated interaction and reciprocity, including behaviour that does not depend on formulating a moral principle (Trivers 1971). Comparative ethnographic research identifies recurring patterns in moral assessment: coded records from sixty societies showed broadly positive evaluations of seven forms of cooperation, including helping kin, reciprocity, bravery, fair division, and respect for prior possession. The regularity concerns these cooperative forms within the available records (Curry, Mullins, and Whitehouse 2019).

passages.heading: 4-the-natural-and-social-sciences-on-valuation
passages.section: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation
passages.text: 4.3 Income, needs and well-being

passages.heading: 4-the-natural-and-social-sciences-on-valuation
passages.section: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation
passages.text: Well-being research distinguishes evaluative judgments about one’s life from reports of experienced affect. Studies of income examine associations with both, with results that vary across measures and participants; the earlier disagreement about a plateau in emotional well-being illustrates the importance of those distinctions (Kahneman and Deaton 2010; Killingsworth 2021; Killingsworth, Kahneman, and Mellers 2023). Individual differences, national comparisons, and change over time also pose different empirical questions (Easterlin 1974).

passages.heading: 4-the-natural-and-social-sciences-on-valuation
passages.section: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation
passages.text: Self-determination theory examines autonomy, competence, and relatedness as basic psychological needs. It relates their satisfaction to intrinsic motivation, self-regulation, and well-being, and investigates how social conditions support or frustrate these processes. This supplies an account of how motivation and personal development depend on conditions of learning and participation, alongside the investigation of material resources and reported experience (Ryan and Deci 2000).

passages.heading: 4-the-natural-and-social-sciences-on-valuation
passages.section: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation
passages.text: 4.4 Trust and social outcomes

passages.heading: 4-the-natural-and-social-sciences-on-valuation
passages.section: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation
passages.text: Economic and social research examines associations between generalised trust, institutions, investment, and growth. In the survey measure used by Zak and Knack, trust is the proportion of respondents in a country who agree that most people can be trusted. It records a general reported expectation about others, which can be compared with economic and institutional outcomes. Distinguishing the report from observed conduct clarifies what the measure contributes to an investigation of relationships (Zak and Knack 2001).

passages.heading: 4-the-natural-and-social-sciences-on-valuation
passages.section: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation
passages.text: 4.5 Prices, production and welfare

passages.heading: 4-the-natural-and-social-sciences-on-valuation
passages.section: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation
passages.text: Economic measurement distinguishes prices, production aggregates such as GDP, and measures of household income and consumption. Assessing material living standards requires attention to household resources and their distribution; accounting for unpaid household work can also make otherwise omitted contributions visible. Wider assessments of social progress examine health, education, relationships, political participation, environmental conditions, and insecurity. The choice and aggregation of indicators depend on what the assessment is intended to represent (Stiglitz, Sen, and Fitoussi 2009). Prices and output thus answer questions about exchange and production, while welfare assessment asks how resources and other conditions bear on people’s lives. These measures have distinct meanings from usefulness-value as examined in §1.5.

passages.heading: 4-the-natural-and-social-sciences-on-valuation
passages.section: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation
passages.text: 4.6 Specified objectives and artificial intelligence

passages.heading: 4-the-natural-and-social-sciences-on-valuation
passages.section: 4. The Natural and Social Sciences on Valuation
passages.text: Artificial intelligence research documents cases in which an agent satisfies a specified objective through behaviour that defeats the designer’s purpose. Specification gaming exposes a mismatch between a rewarded proxy and the intended outcome. It motivates better specifications, oversight, and evaluation of effects beyond the rewarded signal (Amodei et al. 2016; Krakovna et al. 2020). Its relevance to the problem of evaluative error in §1.7 is a limited analogy: satisfying a stated objective need not amount to correct evaluation. The immediate question is whether the objective adequately represents the intended good.

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: 5. Comparison of the Answers

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: The traditions differ both in what they call value and in what they ask an account of value to explain. Comparison is most useful when it follows specific questions about grounds, recognition, development, evidence, what endures or changes, and the scope of comparison. A single label such as objective, spiritual, or scientific leaves many of these differences unresolved.

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: 5.1 Grounds, evidence, change and comparison

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Question Madhyasth Darshan Advaita Vedanta Western philosophical approaches Natural and social sciences What grounds value or fulfilment? Essentiality of active units in coexistence; human understanding and fulfilment through jeevan The Self, identical with Brahman, as the ground of dearness and fullness; finite goods retain empirical significance (§2.1) Competing accounts through goods, reasons, attitudes, nature, or practical construction Investigated mechanisms, conditions, and outcomes; normative standards stated for particular assessments How can evaluation be mistaken? Over-, under-, or mis-evaluation under delusion Ignorance and superimposition; attachment and failures of discrimination False judgment, distorted response, bad information, or defective reasoning, depending on theory Bias, measurement error, learning failures, and mistaken causal inference How does the evaluator develop? Study of meaning, qualitative refinement across the five faculties, self-evaluation, and evidence in conduct Ethical discipline, non-attachment, hearing, reflection, and contemplation Moral education, practical reasoning, attention, character, and social formation in different theories Learning and development studied through observable interventions and outcomes What is evidence in living? Understood meaning, fulfilled relationships, useful work, and mutual satisfaction Disciplined action and preparation; knowledge that removes ignorance Warranted reasons and judgments, and conduct assessed under the theory’s standards Publicly inspectable observations, measurements, comparisons, and causal tests What endures, and what changes with circumstance? Established, human, and jeevan values endure; means and occasions vary. Usefulness has both constancy and temporality claims whose reconciliation remains open (§§1.5, 5.7, 7.5). Knowledge discloses the Self’s enduring freedom; acquired goods and experiences are transient. Their uses and conditions vary within empirical life (§§2.1, 2.4–2.5). Scheler’s value order supplies an objective standard while recognition develops; economic and capability assessments vary with circumstances of use, exchange, and opportunity (§§3.7–3.8, 5.7). Cooperation shows recurring patterns; psychological needs inform well-being research. Valuation and well-being vary, with findings assessed across populations, periods, and measures (§§4.1–4.3). In what sense can values be compared, and what does comparison not licence? Dedication, endurance, inclusion, and common or complete value distinguish relations; they do not establish exchange rates or general compensation between value classes (§5.6). Liberation has ultimate priority; dharma governs finite pursuits. This ordering supplies neither a numerical exchange rate nor every allocation decision (§§2.2, 2.4, 5.6). Ranking can occur without common measurement; dignity and appropriate modes of valuation constrain exchange. Comparability alone does not establish permissible compensation or trade-offs (§§3.6–3.8, 5.6). Measures compare choices and outcomes for stated purposes; neural common scales and welfare aggregation do not by themselves justify moral equivalence or trade-offs (§§4.1, 4.5–4.6).

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: 5.2 Essentiality and normative authority

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan’s identification of value with essential participation (§1.1) meets Hume’s question about the warrant for moving from what is to what ought to be (§3.2). Natural-law and realist approaches likewise offer grounds independent of actual approval, while differing over human nature and normative authority. The comparison concerns why a particular account of participation should guide conduct and how it addresses dependency or disagreement (§7.4).

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Advaita locates primary dearness in the Self and ultimate fulfilment in knowledge of Brahman. This differs from locating value in each active unit’s essential participation. Derivative dearness concerns why persons and goods are loved; dependence on Brahman concerns their ultimate reality. Neither claim alone settles the Western question whether a finite good has intrinsic value within empirical life (§§2.1, 3.1).

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: 5.3 Activity, properties and evaluative response

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan distinguishes value in unit activity from its recognition by jeevan (§§1.1–1.4); fitting-attitude theories distinguish actual approval from the response a good warrants (§3.4). Both make correctness a further question about an evaluation. A neural common scale, by contrast, compares options for a decision (§4.1). It describes how selection is implemented without supplying the standard by which over-, under-, or mis-evaluation relative to essentiality would be corrected. The comparison concerns what makes a response appropriate, alongside the mechanisms through which it occurs.

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: The rope–snake illustration makes the difference in correction concrete. Ordinary correction identifies the rope in both accounts. Madhyasth Darshan uses the mistake to illustrate mis-evaluation relative to what the unit is (SB, PDF p. 146). Advaita also uses corrected rope–snake error to explain how knowledge removes error, extending the analogy to knowledge of the Self’s identity with Brahman (BSB, 1.1.4). The wider standards differ: correct recognition and participation within real coexistence, and removal of superimposed limitation through non-dual knowledge (§§1.7, 2.3).

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: 5.4 Establishment, expression and learning

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Establishment in Madhyasth Darshan concerns understood relationship value becoming a sustained basis of fulfilment (§§1.3–1.4, 1.8). Advaita gives virtues and disciplined conduct a preparatory role in knowledge; its purposes and dearness distinctions do not supply counterparts to the darshan’s established–expressed activity pairs (§§2.1–2.2, 2.6). Western accounts of character and care examine practical judgment, attention, and responsiveness (§§3.5, 3.9). These accounts disagree over the understanding that conduct should express and the evidence of its development.

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Research on learning and psychological needs examines changing expectations and the motivational conditions of competence and participation (§§4.1, 4.3). It can inform investigation of value education through performance, reports, and the conditions under which learning persists. The darshan’s further claim to established understanding requires assessment of the meaning understood and responsibilities fulfilled, including how these become continuous (§7.8).

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: 5.5 Happiness, bliss and material provision

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: The four harmonies in Madhyasth Darshan are constituted by activities of jeevan (§1.2), while Advaita’s ananda concerns Brahman’s undivided fullness disclosed through knowledge (§§2.1, 2.4). Their difference concerns what fulfilment is and how it relates to active participation. Western welfare theories further distinguish pleasure, desire satisfaction, and objective goods (§3.5).

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Well-being research separates evaluative judgments about life from experienced affect and examines their associations with income and psychological needs (§4.3). Improved reports can inform an assessment of living conditions; they do not alone establish a specified faculty harmony or knowledge of Brahman. Testing a proposed correspondence requires both a clear account of the claimed fulfilment and measures appropriate to it. Decisions about compensation among goods also require more than a measured rise in satisfaction (§7.1).

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: 5.6 Ordering and value recognition

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan’s dedication, endurance, inclusion, and common or complete relationship value distinguish relations of purpose, persistence, comprehensiveness, and relational scope (§1.6). Scheler’s hierarchy and Hartmann’s distinction between height and strength of demand offer different criteria for ordering (§3.7). Their comparison turns on what each relation licenses in action. Dedication supplies no numerical exchange rate, and inclusion does not by itself permit additional output to compensate for damaged trust. Ranking, common measurement, and permissible compensation remain distinct questions (§3.6); a stated order still needs worked procedures for disputed obligations (§§7.1, 7.7).

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Advaita orders human purposes through liberation’s unproduced freedom and the governance of finite pursuits by dharma (§§2.2, 2.4). Liberation’s priority does not mean that it contains acquired wealth or enjoyment as the darshan’s more comprehensive fulfilment retains preceding content. Material means can support inquiry without reproducing the particular dedication sequence of usefulness, need, and relationship values. This is an ordering of purposes and their conditions, with no numerical equivalence between them. It can reject a pursuit incompatible with duty while leaving the allocation among legitimate material needs to further practical judgment.

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: 5.7 Useful things, labour and symbolic value

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan and Marx distinguish usefulness from monetary appearance and give labour a central role in production and exchange (§§1.5, 3.8). Marx analyses the social form and magnitude of commodity value; the darshan evaluates production and exchange through need, prosperity, and right-use. Their criticisms of exploitation accordingly differ in explanation and remedy.

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Advaita addresses useful things through empirical need, duty, and attachment (§2.5). Food can nourish and work can sustain life, although neither produces liberation. Objects’ dependence on Brahman does not cancel these empirical distinctions. The Advaita passages examined here supply no doctrine of usefulness-constancy and do not specify how labour measures economic value or determines price. Marx therefore supplies a comparison concerning commodity production and magnitude, while Advaita supplies a comparison concerning the ends of acquisition and the limits of the fulfilment sought through it.

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Economic measurement records prices and output, including GDP; these do not measure the darshan’s usefulness value (§4.5). The capability approach asks whether resources become real opportunities for differently situated people (§3.8). Separating capacities, their deployment, realised benefit, and price may help investigate the darshan’s constancy and temporality claims, but remains an analytical proposal to test against the passages (§7.5). These distinctions also expose practical questions for a labour-valued exchange order (§7.11).

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: 5.8 Relationships, agreement and conflict

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Justice in Madhyasth Darshan requires recognised responsibilities and actual fulfilment before mutual satisfaction. Care and recognition theories offer parallel questions about dependency, responsiveness, and practical standing.

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: In Advaita, husband, wife, and child are dear for the Self, while relational duties retain their force within vyavahara without independent ultimate status (BU, 2.4.5; §§2.2, 2.5–2.6). Family Relationships and Values, §2.1, develops the relation between householder discipline and renunciation.

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Survey trust concerns a reported expectation about other people (§4.4). The darshan’s trust is an established relationship value, common across relationships (samya mulya), whose fulfilment is assessed in justice (§§1.3–1.4). Research on reported trust and cooperation can examine social conditions and outcomes (§§4.2, 4.4); identifying those measures with established trust would require evidence that they capture its specified meaning and fulfilment.

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: The darshan holds that quarrelling involves error on at least one side and that correctly understanding parties do not quarrel (SB, p. 146). Applying this harmony claim to scarce resources, absent parties, and competing legitimate needs requires an account of the allocation to make (§7.7).

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
