passages.text: 5.9 Qualitative evaluation in two applications

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Consider a teacher helping a learner and a family producing food. Both are analytical illustrations of the value map. In teaching, guidance and care are established relationship values; human values such as generosity, kindness, grace, and compassion inform the provision of time, suitable content, and conditions for learning. The learner’s developing understanding is an achievement whose evidence must be examined. The responsibility to guide endures, while the explanation, pace, and resources appropriate to its fulfilment change with the learner’s receptivity (§§1.2–1.4).

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Dedication relates useful teaching materials and expressed conduct to the relationship they serve and to the purpose of resolved living (§1.6). An enjoyable lesson or grateful response does not alone establish that guidance was fulfilled. Assessment should ask whether the learner can explain the meaning and apply it in a new situation, and whether the teacher’s assistance met the actual difficulty. Such evidence can support a claim of learning while leaving continuity of understanding and wider awakening open to examination (§§1.4, 1.8).

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: In food production, usefulness concerns what the produce can fulfil in nourishment. Labour develops that usefulness through cultivation and preparation; aesthetic addition is meaningful where it adds convenience to usefulness. Labour assessment concerns exchange, while price records symbolic valuation. Quantities produced and prices received therefore require interpretation through assessed need, actual provision, and the responsibilities fulfilled, including care for those unable to produce (§§1.3, 1.5).

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: Dedication gives useful production its place in relationships and humane living. A harvest obtained through deception or degradation of soil can exhibit productive competence while leaving trust or responsibility for regeneration unfulfilled. Assessment must examine nourishment, labour, relationships, and continued productive conditions together. Need, harvest seasons, storage, and regeneration introduce temporal circumstances: what is available and how it should be used can change. Distinguishing these circumstances from the produce’s capacities may help investigate the constancy and temporality claims about usefulness, but remains a proposed distinction whose textual adequacy requires examination (§§1.5–1.6, 7.5). Specifying sustainable yields and fair allocation still requires factual investigation and practical reasoning (§§7.9, 7.11).

passages.heading: 5-comparison-of-the-answers
passages.text: The other accounts ask different questions of these scenes. Advaita examines whether teaching and provision fulfil empirical responsibilities without attachment; their performance can prepare for knowledge but does not produce liberation (§§2.4–2.5). Western approaches assess welfare and opportunity, dignity and permissible exchange, or care and responsiveness, according to the theory (§§3.5–3.6, 3.8–3.9). These assessments need not coincide with the darshan’s named relationship values. Scientific investigation can measure learning outcomes, yields, and their consequences under stated purposes (§§4.1, 4.3–4.5). Such evidence informs assessment of the lesson and harvest; whether guidance or care was fulfilled also depends on the applicable account of relationship and responsibility.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: 6. Critical Review

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: 6.1 Madhyasth Darshan — participation as the standard of value

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The account identifies value with the essentiality of active units and distinguishes this ground from its human recognition and fulfilment. Its objectivity claim thereby has definite content in participation, while allowing error in understanding and limitations in the means of fulfilment.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The five-faculty account supplies constitutive relations for the four harmonies and connects established values with their expressions in conduct. It distinguishes constitutional capacity, understood fulfilment, and evidence of achievement, so attraction, skilled performance, and a claim of inward assurance can each be assessed in its proper role.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Justice requires normative standards, actual fulfilment, and mutual satisfaction. Kindness, grace, and compassion address need and receptivity; labour evaluation, right-use, and rightful receiving address material conditions.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The sixfold articulation of knowledge connects lawful operation and balance with justice, resolution, and truth. It allows technical effectiveness, relational fulfilment, and overall purpose to be examined together while preserving their different responsibilities.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Self-examination and evidence in relationships and work supply criteria of evaluation. The texts acknowledge learning within a disordered tradition and distinguish reported achievements from a wider institutional order still to be realised.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The identity of essentiality and value requires a defence that an interlocutor can assess without first accepting the whole ontology. It remains necessary to explain why a proposed form of participation has normative authority and how competing accounts can be adjudicated.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Complete correctness is connected with awakening, while awakening is recognised through correct understanding and conduct. The account has educational entry points, but a public method for resolving disagreement about an individual’s claimed establishment still needs specification.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Dedication, endurance, inclusion, and completeness distinguish ways values are related, but they do not yet determine allocation in every case of scarce resources and legitimate competing claims. Their domains and practical implications need inspectable decisions without treating disagreement itself as proof of inferior standing.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Reports of successful education and living are evidence to investigate, rather than independent demonstrations of universal efficacy. The claims concerning jeevan, continuity, and institutional scale need distinct forms of verification.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Saturation and constitutional completeness are philosophical commitments whose relation to contemporary physical and biological explanations remains to be established. An activity model can clarify their connections but does not independently verify them or explain a transition to anubhav merely by naming a feedback process.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan offers a connected theory of value in participation; its further development depends on publicly assessable warrants and worked applications of its own standards.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: 6.2 Advaita Vedanta — liberation and the limits of acquisition

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The distinction between liberation and produced attainments provides a sustained account of why acquisition and pleasurable experience may fail to answer the deepest question of fulfilment.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Ethical preparation and action without attachment give the transformation of the evaluator a practical role. Teachings on compassion and loka-sangraha preserve responsibilities within empirical life.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Primary dearness of the Self and the analysis of superimposition connect what people seek with how they understand themselves. This challenges identification of fulfilment with the possessions and experiences of a presently conceived individual ego.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The account’s ultimate ground depends on non-duality and the authority of the means of knowledge through which it is disclosed. The move from familiar dearness to the non-dual Self requires argument in a comparison that does not presuppose that ground.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The relation between empirical responsibilities and ultimate non-doership needs careful interpretation when used to guide institutions, conflict resolution, or distribution. The cited teachings give ethical direction without supplying every institutional detail.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The claim that produced goods cannot provide ultimate fulfilment does not alone determine their comparative importance within finite lives. Further practical reasoning is needed to assess particular relationships and material needs.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Advaita Vedanta connects dearness, mistaken identification, and the ordering of human purposes; its account of ultimate fulfilment leaves further work in specifying the comparative claims of finite goods.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: 6.3 Western value theory — distinctions and competing explanations

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The distinctions between intrinsic and final value, welfare and moral rightness, ranking and commensurability, and actual and fitting attitudes prevent several different questions from being answered by one ambiguous use of value.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Realist, constructivist, phenomenological, care, and capability approaches supply substantive alternatives to simple preference accounts. Evaluator development and the social conditions of fulfilment are well represented within this range.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Arguments concerning dignity, exploitation, recognition, and capabilities make distribution and vulnerability central concerns rather than consequences to be considered only after an abstract theory is complete.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Rival accounts disagree about the grounds of value and the standards of correct response. No single position can be assessed as the settled Western answer.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The separation of metaethics, welfare, action, and political economy can leave difficult work in explaining how their results fit together. Conceptual clarity within one inquiry does not automatically produce a coherent account of living.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Each proposal must show how its standards are known and applied. Appeals to appropriate attitudes, ideal reasoning, flourishing, or intuition relocate this evidential burden rather than removing it.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Western value theory supplies exact distinctions and substantial rival explanations that a comparative account must address individually.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: 6.4 The sciences — mechanisms, outcomes and explanatory limits

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Empirical methods make claims about learning, provision, health, trust, and institutions answerable to evidence beyond an advocate’s testimony.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The distinction between reported experience, life evaluation, behaviour, and measured conditions enables more discriminating tests of claims about well-being.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Reanalysis and conflicting findings can improve an account, as the income–well-being debate illustrates. This capacity for correction is a resource for studying value education and institutional proposals.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Operational measures need an explicit connection to the philosophical claim being tested. The measures reviewed here do not operationalise established relationship values or adjudicate the darshan’s usefulness-constancy claim; those comparisons require an account of what would count as evidence.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Associations do not establish causes, and findings in particular populations do not immediately establish universal regularities. Claims about education or prosperity need appropriate designs and limits.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Empirical success in predicting a choice does not settle whether it is justified; neither a neural common scale nor successful aggregation establishes moral equivalence. Selecting and weighting outcomes requires normative reasoning, and failure of an objective proxy does not by itself establish value pluralism.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The sciences can test many consequences of a value theory while leaving the justification of its fundamental standards to a wider argument.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: 7. Open Problems

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: 7.1 What ordering do the values permit?

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: The darshan’s relations of dedication, endurance, inclusion, and common or complete value already provide distinct grounds for discussing order (§1.6). Dedication identifies a purpose served; endurance concerns persistence or non-transformation; inclusion concerns comprehensiveness; commonness and completeness characterise relationship values. The four harmonies also have cumulative fulfilment in living. The remaining question is what decision rules these relations support, individually and together. Their distinct domains must be preserved before they can guide an allocation or establish priority.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: A gain in productive capacity alongside damaged trust is a useful test: what requires repair, how should resources support that repair, and what would count as restored fulfilment? Further cases should test whether endurance determines priority between competing needs, what inclusion entails for the fulfilment of an included value, and how love’s completeness guides a particular responsibility. These questions concern the practical consequences of the stated relations; a numerical scale of exchange or a general rule of compensation cannot be assumed from their presence.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: 7.2 How can claimed awakening be assessed without circular authority?

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: Self-evaluation, examination of both sides of a relationship, study, and observable conduct are already available resources (MVD, p. 87; JV, pp. 98, 139). The accounts of sanskar, learning through meaningful participation, and study of meaning supply educational entry points (§1.8). They answer the strongest claim that no learning is possible before complete awakening.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: The unresolved question concerns contested authority. When a teacher claims established understanding and a learner finds an apparent error, what shared procedure determines whether the difficulty lies in the teaching, the learner, or the application? The distinction between knowing the more developed and measuring it by an inadequate existing measure allows inquiry; it should not make a claim of development immune to correction (KD, p. 37). Documented explanations, outcomes, counterexamples, and the learner’s freedom to question should be made part of a worked account.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: The four harmonies have definite constitutive relations within the darshan (§1.2). Uncertainty about whether an observer has established their presence in a particular person concerns evidence. It does not make those relations indeterminate. Equally, a person’s report of pleasure, calm, satisfaction, or bliss must be interpreted in context before it can establish the specified faculty harmony. A useful assessment should examine the person’s reasons, freedom from contradiction in the relevant activity, fulfilled responsibilities, and continuity across circumstances, while keeping ordinary self-description distinct from the full claim of realised understanding.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: 7.3 How does mutual satisfaction include everyone affected?

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: Justice requires recognised relationships, value-fulfilment, evaluation, and mutual satisfaction. It already asks more than whether two people consent. A further account should show how to assess relationships where one person cannot communicate a judgment, lacks relevant information, or depends on the evaluator for care.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: The appropriate tests include a young child, an adult requiring continuing support, and an agreement whose effects fall on absent neighbours. Actual provision and fulfilled responsibilities must matter alongside expressed assent. Satisfaction within the immediate pair cannot alone establish that obligations to other affected people have been fulfilled (§1.4).

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: 7.4 What warrants the identification of essentiality and value?

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: The texts explicitly identify essentiality, essential nature, and value, and connect human dharma with happiness and humane participation (MVD, pp. 47, 124–125; SB, pp. 50, 87). The question is therefore the warrant for a stated identification, rather than the recovery of a missing definition.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: A further argument should explain how essential participation is distinguished from a merely recurrent behaviour and why that participation provides a reason for action. It should also explain what would count against an asserted identification. Otherwise a dispute about the good can be redescribed as a dispute about essentiality without making the original disagreement easier to resolve.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: The effort–motion–result account makes this question sharper. Effective power and persistent activity occur in both humane and inhumane conduct. The further warrant must concern the character and fulfilment of that activity, rather than its efficacy alone. Likewise, natural lawfulness and balance cannot establish a particular human obligation without the intervening account of relationships, knowledge, and humane purpose (§§1.1, 1.8).

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: 7.5 In what sense is usefulness constant?

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: The primary passages contain a difference that a complete account must address. Usefulness is described as definite through the example of a kilogram of wheat across a hundred years, together with a claim that interference can reduce its value (JV, p. 123). Object value is also called constant through the sesame example (JV, pp. 137–138). Usefulness and beauty are expressly called temporal (samayik) in relation to changing needs, use, exchange, and deployment, and contrasted with enduring established, human, and jeevan values (MAD, reader p. 51). Both claims are stated in §1.5. The task is first textual: identify the sense and conditions of each claim before proposing their reconciliation.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: Distinguishing a thing’s capacities, its transformation through labour or interference, the benefit realised in a situation, and its price may help analyse the difference. A quantity of grain can retain a nutritive capacity while its condition, access, and the need it serves change. These distinctions are analytical proposals; the cited passages do not expressly supply them as their reconciliation. A fuller treatment should test the proposed reading against both passages and further uses of the terms, including what remains constant when interference reduces usefulness.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: 7.6 How complete are the value lists and pairings?

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: The nine principal established relationship values and their nine corresponding expressions have explicit primary support in MAD reader p. 30. The principal classification need not remain uncertain because JV p. 108 introduces its list with illustrative wording. The remaining work concerns the relation of this classification to other contextual lists and to the larger activity enumeration.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: The 122 activity members do not establish 122 distinct names or 122 separate relationship values. A concordance should preserve the difference between a value class, an activity position, a paired expression, and evidence in conduct. Repeated terms such as generosity and contextual uses of happiness or bliss require definitions and context. A named position at one faculty also cannot be read as a claim that understanding the corresponding value needs that faculty alone (§§1.2–1.3).

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: 7.7 How are rival legitimate obligations resolved?

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: The claim that correct parties do not quarrel supplies the darshan’s position on harmony (SB, p. 146). Recognition, mutual fulfilment, and common resolution are its proposed direction. The difficult case is a conflict between legitimate needs when existing means are insufficient: two patients need the only available treatment, or protecting one community shifts a burden to another.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: A worked account should identify relevant facts, responsibilities, available alternatives, and the reason for its allocation. It should distinguish a remediable error from a material limit that remains after misunderstanding is corrected. This would show how the harmony claim guides action and how unavoidable loss is acknowledged, rather than treating the existence of disagreement as a completed diagnosis.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: 7.8 How does outward learning become establishment and continuity?

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: The texts connect sanskar, understood meaning, practice, self-evaluation, and the acceptance of evidenced conduct with further expression (MVD, pp. 83, 90, 94; KD, pp. 84, 112–113). They distinguish intermittent meaningful conduct from continuity. These resources support a positive educational account across the activities of jeevan, including the learner’s visualisation, desire, understanding, and resolve (§1.8).

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: The further task is to document the transition. Constitutional completeness identifies an inherent capacity; establishment concerns understood value in state; fulfilment expresses it through activity; continuity concerns its sustained evidence across circumstances. What differentiates instructed performance, independently understood fulfilment, and such continuity? How are relapse, conflicting incentives, and mistaken self-assessment recognised? An educational route beginning with outward participation should be examined as a pedagogical interpretation, without presenting it as a prescribed sequence or repetition as a sufficient cause of awakening. Evidence should include the learner’s explanation and self-examination as well as conduct and its effects, with each claim assessed against the faculty activity or relationship it concerns.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: The continuity from action through evaluation to revised understanding also requires discrimination between several outcomes. A learner can correct a technique, recognise a responsibility, clarify a concept, or claim anubhav; each calls for appropriate evidence. An account of qualitative refinement should explain how such changes affect subsequent participation. It should preserve the distinction between a definite constitutive relation of harmony and the process through which that harmony is achieved and evidenced in a particular person.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: 7.9 How does value across the four orders guide ecological decisions?

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: The darshan attributes value to every unit, directs humans towards nurture, and relates resource use to regeneration. It also describes vitalising and devitalising effects in relation to living bodies, including human bodies (SB, pp. 141, 179–182, 200–201). These commitments cannot be reduced either to unrestricted human preference or to a fully specified theory of non-human rights.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: Further work should examine habitat loss, competing forms of life, restoration times, and effects on future people. The account must explain how participation and regeneration are assessed when there is no single immediate beneficiary and when one useful activity disrupts another form of coexistence.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: 7.10 What evidence supports the educational and institutional claims?

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: Self-examination, fulfilled relationships, useful work, and reported educational results supply different kinds of evidence. Nagraj’s accounts include learning and self-experimentation, while the discussion of exchange in Adhyatmvad distinguishes reported achievements in production, prosperity, and justice from the wider exchange order still awaited at the time of writing (JV, pp. 98, 139; SB, p. 294; AVD, p. 52).

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: These historical reports should not be presented as proof that the full institutional order was implemented or as a statement of its present reach. Longitudinal studies could examine learning, sustained conduct, provision, and relationships, with explicit measures and comparison conditions. Institutional evaluation should separately examine distribution, ecological effects, dependency, and the ability to correct failures. Such research would test specified claims without assuming that a questionnaire exhausts jeevan or that inward evaluation forbids external investigation.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: 7.11 How should labour be evaluated and provision distributed?

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: Labour deployment, labour-value assessment, protection from exploitation, and profit-and-loss-free exchange are explicit commitments (MVD, pp. 260, 268–269; SB, p. 237). The next questions concern their implementation: how should differences of skill, effort, training, risk, tools, time, quality, and productivity enter an assessment? What happens when socially necessary care yields no exchangeable product, or when a useful product depends on accumulated knowledge contributed by many people?

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: Remuneration, gift, and award already widen the account of rightful wealth beyond an individual’s immediate production (AVD, p. 170). A developed allocation procedure should explain provision for children, older people, people with disabilities, and anyone temporarily unable to work. It should also distinguish the evaluation of labour from the urgency of need and from the basic standing of the person who receives support.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: 7.12 How are equal human standing and unequal development related?

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: The account recognises common human purpose and capacity while distinguishing levels of understanding and conduct. Developmental differences can matter when assigning a task or assessing competence. They do not by themselves justify differences in basic worth, protection, or the right to question a judgment.

passages.heading: 7-open-problems
passages.text: A full treatment should show how conferred rights and duties are applied to less experienced learners and people whose capacities differ. It should make clear how recognition and care protect a person’s standing while their understanding or productive ability is still developing. This is especially important wherever claims of higher value or awakening carry authority within a family, educational setting, or institution.

passages.heading: 8-conclusion
passages.text: 8. Conclusion

passages.heading: 8-conclusion
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan identifies value with essentiality in coexistence. Units are activity, and their form, properties, essential nature, and dharma concern aspects of that participation. A unit’s value is present through its essentiality; human recognition can understand it correctly or mistake it. Awakening concerns the development of understanding and fulfilment in the active conscious unit, jeevan.

passages.heading: 8-conclusion
passages.text: The structural account specifies what this fulfilment comprises. Happiness, peace, contentment, and bliss are harmonies between defined faculty activities. Established values in state have corresponding expressions in motion, while justice joins recognition of relationships, value-fulfilment, evaluation, and mutual satisfaction. Constitutional capacity, achieved harmony, and evidence of attainment remain distinct. Their distinction allows education to acknowledge meaningful participation while examining the understanding and continuity it demonstrates.

passages.heading: 8-conclusion
passages.text: The value classes connect these harmonies with human conduct, relationships, useful things, aesthetic addition, and symbolic valuation. Their ordering involves dedication, endurance, inclusion, and common or complete relationship value, each with its own domain. Evaluation must identify which value is at issue, what fulfilment it calls for, and in what sense time or comparison applies. The difference between the texts’ constancy and temporality claims about usefulness remains a question for further collation and argument.

passages.heading: 8-conclusion
passages.text: Advaita locates dearness in the Self, identical with Brahman, while Madhyasth Darshan locates value in units’ essentiality. Western theories distinguish grounds, welfare, and exchange; the scientific studies reviewed here test mechanisms and outcomes without supplying the darshan’s classes of mulya. These comparisons sharpen the questions of normative warrant, disputed authority, dependency, allocation, and public evidence. The darshan’s contribution is a connected account of value’s ground, its constitution in activity, and its fulfilment in living. Further work must show how its distinct ordering relations guide difficult decisions and how claims of established understanding are assessed through explanation, conduct, and sustained participation.

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: Appendix: Structural formalisation of value

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: A.1 Harmony as a constitutive relation

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: The following notation makes two relations in §§1.2–1.4 explicit: what constitutes a named jeevan value, and what fulfils value in a relationship. The definitions come from the primary texts; the predicates and their logical organisation are an analytical reconstruction (MVD, pp. 327–328, 331, 333, 346; JV, p. 138; MAD, reader p. 47).

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: Let j denote a jeevan in its current activity, and m,v,c,b,a its faculties mun, vritti, chitta, buddhi, and atma. Write Hxy(j) for the source-defined harmony between faculties x and y, including its understood content. Thus vritti–chitta harmony requires resolved, just thought and desire in accord. Agreement between mistaken beliefs is insufficient. The four naming relations are:

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: Sukh(j)≡Hmv(j),Shanti(j)≡Hvc(j),Santosh(j)≡Hcb(j),Anand(j)≡Hba(j).

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: Here ≡ records a constitutive identification: the named value is the harmony lived and felt in these activities. Structural definiteness concerns what the value consists in. Whether a particular person presently fulfils that relation is a further question, and what evidence establishes that fulfilment is a third. The constitution of jeevan supplies the capacities whose coordinated, awakened activity fulfils the harmonies (§1.2).

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: Write AΣ(j) for realisation of coexistence in atma, where Σ denotes satta. Ultimate bliss, paramanand, belongs to this realisation and its evidence (MVD, pp. 327–328). Eternal saturation and concurrence with satta concern the ontological relation already present; AΣ(j) concerns its realisation in awakened activity. Evaluation and feeling belong to the sentient unit saturated in actionless chetana (MVD, pp. 35, 74–75; SB, pp. 63–64). This distinction keeps inherent capacity, actual awakening, and the reality realised separately identifiable within their connection.

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: A.2 Definite expectations and evaluated fulfilment

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: Let r denote an actual relationship between participating persons and Nr its value requirements towards completeness. These requirements are grounded in the relationship and its established values. A participant can desire something that misrepresents them. The resources, abilities, and concrete acts needed for fulfilment depend on circumstances. In a voluntary contact, the specified expectations also enter the assessment and remain answerable to justice (MVD, pp. 61–62; MAD, reader p. 51).

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: Four predicates preserve the stated structure of justice:

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: Predicate Meaning in an instance of participation Rr The relationship and its value requirements are correctly recognised. Fr Actual participation fulfils those requirements through appropriate acts and means. Er Evaluation correctly determines what has been fulfilled, examining both sides. Mr Mutual satisfaction is present in the recognised and evaluated fulfilment.

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: The complete criterion is represented as:

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: Jr:=Rr∧Fr∧Er∧Mr.

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: The conjunction records the four requirements together. Their practical order remains recognition, fulfilment, evaluation, and mutual satisfaction. Deliberation before action assesses the responsibility, available means, and proposed contribution; evaluation of accomplished participation examines actual fulfilment (MVD, pp. 311, 336; JV, pp. 98, 138–139). A coherent plan may correctly identify the responsibility while Fr remains unfulfilled. Reported satisfaction likewise needs examination alongside recognition, conduct, and its result.

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: The same jeevan recognises, evaluates, and tastes value. Inner harmony and fulfilled mutuality are therefore connected through the activity of the participating persons. The texts place happiness, peace, contentment, and bliss in the experience of established values (JV, pp. 138–139; MAD, reader p. 51). One fulfilled relationship provides evidence about that participation; continuity and comprehensive awakening require evidence across the wider field of living. The criterion keeps the understood basis, the contribution actually made, and its evaluated fulfilment available for separate examination.

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: A.3 Orderliness, continuity and evidence

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: Fulfilled value extends into work and social participation. Law, regulation, and balance concern the organisation of means; justice, dharma, and truth concern recognised relationships, resolved purpose, and realised understanding (MVD, pp. 80, 137, 156, 174). Inner harmony has its evidence in resolution, family prosperity, social fearlessness, and participation in universal orderliness (JV, pp. 53, 62, 140; AVD, p. 228; KD, pp. 112–113). Each field calls for its own examination: a person’s assurance, a family’s adequate provision, and society-wide fearlessness make claims of different scope.

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: Evaluation can clarify the basis of subsequent participation. An unfulfilled responsibility may disclose mistaken recognition, inadequate means, or a conflict requiring resolution; successful participation may strengthen an understood acceptance (§§1.4, 1.8). These changes concern understanding and conduct within the constitutionally complete jeevan. The notation specifies the content that development must fulfil. Explaining how learning proceeds, how long it takes, and how realisation occurs requires a further account of development (§7.8).

passages.heading: appendix-structural-formalisation-of-value
passages.text: Evidence about a harmony also differs from the harmony itself. An observer may have incomplete evidence about Hxy(j) while its meaning remains definite. A record can mark a claim as supported, contradicted, or not yet established; these describe the assessment of a claim. First-person examination, explanations, actual conduct, fulfilled responsibilities, and continuity across relevant circumstances contribute distinct evidence. Examining them together connects the definite account of value with the assessment of particular persons and practices (§§7.2, 7.8, 7.10).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Appendix: Quick Glossary

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Term Use in this study Mulya Value: the essentiality of an active unit in coexistence; recognised, evaluated, and experienced through the activities of jeevan. Maulikta Essentiality or fundamental distinctiveness, understood through essential nature and dharma. Swabhav / dharma Essential nature / order-specific innateness, inseparable from the unit; human dharma is happiness. Jeevan Conscious unit with the faculties atma, buddhi, chitta, vritti, and mun. Sthiti / gati State / motion, inseparable aspects of activity, rather than successive stages. Bal / shakti Strength / power, corresponding to state and motion. Sampriktata / urja-sampannata Saturation in Omnipresence / the energy-fullness of units grounded in that saturation. Mool cheshta Basic impulsion, expressed as the activity of effort, motion, and result. Shram–gati–parinam Effort–motion–result, inseparable aspects of continuing unit activity. Chetana / chaitanya Omnipresent, actionless knowledge in relation to sentient nature / sentient nature present as jeevan. Gyan Knowledge: Omnipresence as ground, unfolded through realisation and evidenced in human understanding and living. Niyam–niyantran–santulan Law, regulation, and balance in the connected account of orderliness. Nyaya–dharma–satya Justice, resolution in human thought and participation, and truth as coexistence; unit-dharma also names order-specific innateness. Bhav / samveg Sentiment, defined through essentiality, value, responsibility, and participation / impetus. Also a named activity pair at vritti. Jeevan mulya Happiness, peace, contentment, and bliss as definite harmonies lived and felt in the related activities of jeevan. Samatva / nirvirodh Concurrence / absence of opposition in the specified activities; the structural basis of the named faculty harmonies. Manav mulya Human values expressed through human essential nature and dharma. Sthapit mulya Relationship values borne in bal/sthiti; their establishment in a person concerns understood acceptance, evidenced through fulfilment. Shishta mulya Expressed or civic values: the corresponding expressions in gati, dedicated to the established values. Sambandh / sampark Relationship with expectations predetermined towards completeness / contact with voluntarily determined expectations, both answerable to justice. Mulyankan Evaluation of essentiality, recognised relationships, and fulfilled values. Adhimulyan / avamulyan Over-evaluation / under-evaluation. Nirmulyan The third evaluative error in MVD p. 306, rendered mis-evaluation; vocabulary variants are recorded below. Nirakarshan Freedom from attraction or attachment; in MVD p. 152, freedom from the three evaluative errors. Daya / kripa / karuna Kindness supplying missing content / grace developing missing receptivity / compassion developing both. Eshana Motive or aspiration; the three named motives concern progeny, wealth, and reputation. Prayog / utpadan Application through labour until success / production standardising the successful process. Upyogita mulya Usefulness value: what a thing can fulfil in nourishment, protection, and participation; the texts’ differing temporal claims are distinguished in §§1.5 and 7.5. Object value In the sesame passage, the usefulness value of things; this wording introduces no further class (JV, pp. 137–138). Kala mulya / saundarya mulya Aesthetic value or beauty, meaningful as convenience added to usefulness. Prateek mulya Symbolic value, especially money; an assigned amount does not by itself establish the usefulness of the represented thing. Sadupyog / prayojansheelta Right-use / purposeful-use of means in humane living and its wider purposes. Chitta / chitran Faculty of contemplation and visualisation / its activity of visualisation. Chintan / sakshatkar Contemplation / direct apprehension; in KD p. 84, contemplation concerns justice, dharma, and truth. Bodh / sankalp Understanding at buddhi / resolve to express the understanding. Anubhav / praman Realisation / its evidence in living. Tulan / vishleshan Deliberation or comparison / analysis at vritti. Asvadan / chayan Tasting / selection at mun. Samya mulya / purna mulya Common value, trust / complete value, love, in the principal relationship-value classification. Samarpan Dedication: the relation in which usefulness serves need, and need and value fulfilment serve the further purposes specified in §1.6. Guru mulyan / laghu mulya Higher valuation / lower value; guru mulyan is defined through a long-lasting result or non-transformability. Context distinguishes this criterion from acquisitive exchange and from inclusion across orders. Sanskar Acceptances, understanding, and tendencies towards completeness, evidenced through bodily, verbal, and mental participation. Susanskar / kusanskar Formation towards awakening and resolution / formation towards decline. Aapyayan / parimarjan Internal reception of value, evidenced in evaluation / qualitative refinement in hope, thought, desire, and resolve.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Editorial Notes

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Texts, translations and page conventions

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: This revision uses a targeted comparison of the primary passages cited below, including Hindi where English wording or pagination changes the argument. It is not a complete collation of Nagraj’s corpus. MVD, SB, JV, and AVD page numbers denote PDF positions in the linked files; MVD’s visible page footer agrees with that convention. In JV the printed number is one lower than the PDF position. SB’s retained contents pagination differs from the bilingual PDF pagination.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: KD citations use printed body pages and chapter numbers where specified. The Hindi body page is twenty-five below its PDF position. The working translation’s [p. N] markers introduce the page. Front-matter numbering must be identified separately because it overlaps with body numbering. KD is a working English translation, and AVD is also provisional; neither status is removed by its use here. Important activity and continuity passages in KD pp. 37, 84, and 112–113 were checked against the Hindi page images. MAD denotes the Hindi Manav Abhyas Darshan in the linked native reader. Its references use the displayed page numbers in the 222-page version, not PDF positions or assumed printed-page offsets. The English formulations here paraphrase the Hindi; they are not attributed to an English edition.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Essentiality, activity and the enumeration

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The identification of essentiality with value and its connection with essential nature and dharma are explicit in MVD pp. 47, 124–125, SB pp. 50, 87, and AVD p. 184. The exposition retains this relation without adding a mechanism in which form and properties must first align with the other aspects to produce value. The map in §1.3 organises the principal uses of mulya relevant to human living. It separates usefulness and aesthetic value for explanation and includes symbolic value for comparison with them; MVD p. 306 groups usefulness and aesthetics together, while symbolic value is named separately at p. 183. The map is not an assertion that the corpus supplies seven mutually exclusive classes.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: MVD p. 203 uses bhav-kriya broadly for values and evaluation. MVD p. 338 and AVD p. 92 also identify a particular bhav/samveg pair at vritti. Bhav is defined through essentiality, value, responsibility, and participation; samveg is the impetus associated with meaningful union, whose direction can be towards advancement or decline (MVD, pp. 43, 338). The shared term does not make all value-activity one position at vritti, nor does the pairing establish a universal causal sequence from sentiment to every outward action.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The awakened enumeration has 122 activity members in 61 pairs: two at atma, four at buddhi, sixteen at chitta, thirty-six at vritti, and sixty-four at mun (MVD, p. 323; AVD, p. 91). This counts activity positions, not 122 distinct names or 122 relationship values. The nine established–expressed pairs in §1.3 are a specified part of the account; the enumeration does not classify every activity pair as such a relationship-value pair.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Established and expressed values

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The exposition adopts the one-to-one correspondence of established values in bal/sthiti and expressed, civic, or shishta values in gati. The table retains the paired positions in AVD pp. 91–94 and the definitions in MVD pp. 328–348. The educational formulation that outward expressions can be learnt before establishment in state is an interpretive articulation of the learning route, read with the distinction of state and motion and the accounts of education and evidenced conduct (KD, pp. 18–19, 84, 112–113; SB, pp. 237, 294). It is not presented as a newly located verbatim sentence or a necessary sequence for every learner.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: MAD reader p. 30 explicitly identifies the principal nine established values, their corresponding nine expressions, trust as common value, and love as complete value. This supplies direct classification evidence beyond JV p. 108, which introduces the nine relationship values as examples. KD p. 26 uses an illustrative list including daya, sneha, udarta, gaurav, adar, vatsalya, shraddha, prem, and kritagyata. Six Hindi terms coincide directly with the JV list; adar and samman should not silently be counted as identical. The principal nine-value classification is retained; the illustrative KD list is not silently substituted for it or treated as proof that the principal taxonomy is uncertain. This does not assert that every occurrence of mulya throughout the corpus belongs to those nine values. Naturalness, concordance, humility, and devoutness are running English terms for the relevant expressed values; ordinary English associations do not exhaust their source definitions.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Activity, saturation and the four aspects

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The effort–motion–result alignment follows SB pp. 60–62. The text places effort/strength with dharma and svabhava, motion with svabhava and guna, and result with roop and amaratva. The compressed account in §1.1 concerns aspects of the active unit; amaratva is retained here with its surrounding constitutional-completeness context, rather than generalised into the immortality of every present material configuration. The overlap of svabhava means this is not a one-to-one derivation or a three-stage chronology. No physical potential, numerical force law, or transition equation is inferred from it.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The account of relative power and characteristic participation draws on Technical Note: Four Aspects of the Active Unit, in its discussions of unit activity, the four aspects, order-wise examples, and the limits of a process interpretation. Its rendering of usefulness as functional significance is analytical and does not make every actual effect morally good. The interpretation of dharma as order-specific innateness must distinguish change within an order from a transition between orders. The human case also distinguishes the constitution of jeevan from its current understanding and conduct.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Chetana, chaitanya and knowledge

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: MVD p. 35 names knowledge as chetana in relation to chaitanya; pp. 74–75 distinguish actionless, non-transforming consciousness/knowledge from transformations in nature and identify chaitanya as constitutionally complete jeevan. The exposition does not treat satta as becoming a unit, performing evaluation, or receiving anubhav. Knowledge as omnipresent ground and knowledge realised and evidenced in human living are connected uses, not an additional substance and its transmission. Sentience includes evaluation but is not exhaustively defined by it, and constitutional completeness does not guarantee awakened evaluation. SB pp. 63–64 and 249 supply the distinctions between natural mutuality, sentient capacities, and correct human recognition and fulfilment.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The faculties, qualitative refinement and evidence

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The five-faculty table follows KD §3.8, p. 84’s Hindi account of sthiti/gati. In AVD pp. 91–94 the English strength/power headings are reversed relative to the Hindi; §1.2 follows the checked Hindi relation. Chitta names the faculty, chitran its visualising activity, and chintan its contemplative activity. The integrated exposition describes dependencies of meaning and expression; it does not posit a neural mechanism or a fixed temporal passage through five successive compartments.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: MVD p. 83 presents interdependent relations among language, meaning, evaluation, worldview, and the perceiver’s capacities, returning to language. Words communicate meanings concerning existing realities; what the person apprehends depends on view, evaluation, capacity, ability, and receptivity. These relations concern activities of chitta, whose adequacy depends on understanding. Study of meaning can reach understanding and realisation and become available for renewed expression (MVD, p. 83; KD, pp. 112–113). This is a cycle of apprehension and communication, not a linear causal sequence that generates the value of the indicated unit. Constitutional completeness identifies the capacity of jeevan; it does not establish that a present evaluation is correct.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The realisation–behaviour–application evidences (MVD, p. 12) and the knowledge–law–regulation–balance–justice–dharma–truth passage (p. 174) connect understanding and living without making their terms interchangeable outside that argument. MAD reader p. 45 grounds the account of aapyayan and parimarjan; neither is equated with memorisation or habit formation alone.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: MVD pp. 99–100 distinguish realisation-oriented understanding in study from realisation-based understanding and its expression. Page 156 connects atma with realisation, buddhi–chitta with resolution, and vritti–mun with just behaviour. These relations are not exclusive ownership of justice, dharma, or truth by individual faculties: all three are accepted in buddhi and participate in contemplation and deliberation. The eight dimensions of visualisation on p. 327 describe an activity of chitta, not the production of the imaged unit by a perceiver.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Sixfold knowledge and continuing evaluation

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The continuity of knowledge, law, regulation, balance, justice, dharma, and truth is directly stated in MVD p. 174, with evidence of all six through realisation on p. 80. The natural-order conformance descriptions follow SB pp. 236–237. Their particular illustrations do not allocate each term exclusively to one order. Dharma as innateness and dharma as the humane perspective of resolution in thought are related uses whose distinctions remain necessary (MVD, pp. 125, 137, 156, 174).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: A State-Dynamic Model of Coexistence, §§1–3, 7–8, and 10–11, develops the analytical connection between unit activity, human orientation, consequences, and later evaluation.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The present paper uses that connection to clarify continuing evaluation and learning in §§1.4 and 1.8. The model’s distinction of actual and operatively recognised mutuality and its grouping of consequences into internal, bodily, relational, and natural domains are analytical reconstructions. They do not enlarge configurational parinam into a source-stated definition of every human consequence, or make feedback a sufficient cause of anubhav. The applications in §5.9 use the forms of value, dedication, and temporal distinctions developed in this study.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The model’s grouping into two coupled triads and its projections of niyam–nyaya, niyantran–dharma, and santulan–satya are likewise analytical, non-exclusive mappings. They are not adopted as primary-text identities or faculty assignments. A family or institution is an arrangement of persons, relationships, and work; the evaluators are the participating human beings. No collective jeevan or new ontological unit is inferred from social orderliness.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Harmonies and contextual uses of jeevan values

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The faculty-harmony account in JV p. 138 and MVD p. 327, and the cumulative fulfilment in KD §3.12, p. 112, supply the two columns of the harmony table. The social column preserves the cumulative sequence; it does not assign fearlessness or coexistence alone as an exclusive outward equivalent. Their distinctness supports separate examination, but does not alone prove the impossibility of every aggregate assessment. The formal appendix keeps the named relations distinct because the cited texts supply no numerical scale or exchange rates.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The scope of fulfilment described in §§1.2 and A.3 connects inner satisfaction with self-governed conduct in relationships and wider orderliness (JV, pp. 53, 62, 140; AVD, p. 228; KD, pp. 112–113). This connection does not replace the cumulative fulfilment table with four exclusive correspondences or make a family or society the bearer of a collective jeevan.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: MVD p. 328 locates the named anand activity at buddhi, while p. 323 also uses bliss language at atma. The table follows the specific named positions rather than asserting an exclusive location for every use of bliss. KD p. 37 also speaks of resolution and prosperity as jeevan values in its context. The fourfold list is retained where the four harmonies are the subject; contextual lists are not silently expanded or reduced to force one enumeration. Contentment in MVD p. 331 includes readiness for production beyond need as well as absence of deficiency-sentiment.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: MAD reader p. 47 explicitly equates absence of opposition in each adjacent faculty pair with a named value and with a quality of behaviour, thought, desire, or understanding. This strengthens the constitutive reading adopted in §§1.2 and A.1. Its aparadh-hin is rendered behaviour free of wrongdoing; it is not confined to compliance with a prevailing penal code. Page 51 connects the four harmonies with the experience of established values and describes established values as enduring across time and place. The study’s term structural names these definite relations of activity, rather than a claim about measured anatomy or a new spatial arrangement of the jeevan atom.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: MVD pp. 343 and 346 distinguish sensory pleasantness from happiness defined as resolution. The pedagogical progression from pleasant contact to resolved thought, an understood whole, and realised existence is therefore developed through the specified faculty relations, not adopted as four independent satisfactions. Absence of confusion alone is insufficient if the person’s beliefs misrecognise reality; merely drawing a comprehensive image is insufficient for chitta–buddhi harmony. The eight dimensions of visualisation and the definition of contentment have practical implications for planning; a successful plan alone is not proof of santosh. Feeling the four harmonies is attributed to jeevan, while their named positions remain distinct; the asvadan activity at mun is not made the exclusive location of all four.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The appendix’s harmony predicates, relationship requirements, and conjunction for justice are analytical notation. Their substantive content comes from the cited definitions, not from the symbols themselves. They distinguish constitutive definiteness, an actual person’s state, and an observer’s evidence. No stochastic rule, numerical utility function, automatic passage from logical consistency to fulfilment, or deterministic law of awakening is attributed to the primary texts.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Evaluation errors and non-attachment

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The Hindi sentence on correct evaluation in MVD p. 203 names under- and over-evaluation, whereas its English adds mis-evaluation. The triadic account in §1.7 is therefore cited to MVD pp. 152, 306 and SB p. 146. The illustrations in §1.7 come from SB PDF p. 146, which gives both the rope–snake and iron–gold comparisons in Hindi and English. MVD p. 306 prints nirmulyan (निर्मूल्यन); occurrences of amulyan elsewhere should retain their own source wording. MVD pp. 198–199 distinguishes ativyapti as more, avyapti as other than, and anavyapti as less. English list order is not a safe basis for matching these terms.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The headword translated as dispassion in MVD p. 152 is nirakarshan (निराकर्षण). The exposition uses that headword. It should not be substituted for vairagya in Advaita or for KD’s distinct uses of virag, vairagya, and para-vairagya. The related discussion of non-doership concerns wrongful action, while KD p. 37 describes completeness as continuity of activity.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Human development and relational fulfilment

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: MVD pp. 60–61 fixes the humane and higher-humane triads and the conditions distinguishing kindness, grace, and compassion. SB p. 180 reverses kindness and compassion in the English ordering relative to its Hindi; the exposition follows the checked definitions. SB p. 189 defines heenta through deceit, fraud, duplicity, and hypocrisy. That evaluative term should not be read as a person’s disability or lower productive capacity.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The three motives in MVD p. 319 are eshanas, not the four purusharthas of the Advaita comparison. MVD p. 250’s account of sibling evaluation concerns a pre-adolescent child in an awakened family; it does not establish a universal first onset of evaluation.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The relationship names in MVD p. 190 and the purposes in JV pp. 108–109 are retained without inventing a seven-to-six one-to-one purpose table. In particular, the orderliness relationship is not defined here as a relationship with an abstract entity, nor is master–associate reduced without argument to a modern employment contract. SB p. 237 compresses the justice sequence; MVD pp. 311, 336 supplies the four-part formulation used in §1.4.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Ordering, production and temporal claims

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The relations distinguished in §1.6 come from different arguments. MAD reader p. 34 supplies the dedication of usefulness to need, need to expressed value, expressed to established value, established to human value, and human to jeevan value. The source explicitly names avashyakta mulya. Treating need through the assessment connecting useful means and fulfilled values is this study’s organising choice; its omission as a separate row does not deny that terminology. The usefulness comparison in §1.3 likewise concerns adequacy for a specified need, rather than asserting a numerical measure of essentiality or a rule for comparison across every class. MVD p. 43 defines guru mulyan through long-lasting result or non-transformability. Its inclusion claim at p. 47 concerns the four orders, while pp. 219–222 apply higher and lower value in the account of social participation and followership. MAD reader pp. 30 and 43 identify trust as common value and love as complete value within relationships. These passages warrant distinguishable relations; they do not by themselves supply a single numerical scale, an exchange rate between classes, or a universal inclusion theorem for every row in §1.3. MVD pp. 58 and 67 use higher-for-lower exchange to define acquisitive profit, whose direction must remain distinct from dedication and advancement.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: JV p. 123 calls the usefulness of material objects definite and compares a kilogram of wheat with its counterpart a century earlier, while adding that interference has brought its value down. The sesame example crosses PDF pp. 137–138, calls object value constant, and explicitly identifies it as usefulness value. The alignment in §1.2 and the glossary follows that passage without adding a class to the map. MAD reader p. 51 calls usefulness and beauty temporal, grounding the claim in the temporality of needs, use, exchange, and deployment. §1.5 presents the claims separately and §7.5 examines the textual problem. Describing the first claim as constancy of a kind, or distinguishing inherent capacity from situated use, is a possible interpretation; neither is a reconciliation expressly supplied by these passages. The temporality question also distinguishes a value’s definite content from a person’s present recognition and from the changing means and occasions of its fulfilment.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: MVD p. 56’s endeavour-until-success definition is prayog, translated there as experimentation and rendered application here; the following definition concerns production. SB p. 237’s Hindi differentiates evaluation in justice, labour-value assessment in exchange, and labour deployment in production; its English does not fully reproduce that paragraph.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The extended fear-and-temptation discussion is SB chapter 9, item 11, PDF pp. 290–295, ending before item 12 on p. 295. It is not chapter 11 beginning at PDF p. 199. Its political and educational claims, like MVD p. 199’s account of sentient atoms, are treated as the darshan’s positions rather than independently verified scientific or historical facts. AVD p. 52 is a dated report distinguishing experienced production and justice from the wider exchange system then still awaited.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Comparative terms and verification

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Value in a theory of normative properties, value as essentiality, economic commodity value, and a neural decision variable are not interchangeable senses. The comparisons examine relations between the accounts without treating a shared English word as proof of a shared concept.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The Advaita account brings dearness, human purposes, discrimination, and superimposition into an axiological comparison; these are related concepts, not translations of one technical term equivalent to mulya. Primary and secondary love have direct support in Shankara’s commentary on BU 2.4.5. Reading this as an account of value’s ground is the study’s comparative articulation. Neither derivative dearness nor dependence on Brahman is silently equated with the modern denial of intrinsic empirical value. TU 2.1.1 gives satyam jnanam anantam; the account of being, consciousness, and bliss combines that teaching with 2.7–2.9. Conditioned pleasure does not add to Brahman’s fullness, and the anandamaya sheath in the inward inquiry is not identified with the absolute without qualification.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The four purusharthas are an inherited Indian framework. BG 18.34 groups dharma, kama, and artha in its account of attachment to results; BSB 1.1.1 identifies liberation as the highest human objective. These passages support the Advaita ordering without being presented as one textual enumeration of all four. BG 7.11’s commentary illustrates permissible desire through eating and drinking for bodily maintenance; BG 16.12 condemns unjust acquisition. The governance of finite pursuits by dharma is stated through those constraints. The Vivekachudamani supplies a pedagogical account of discrimination and qualification, with its disputed authorship retained.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: BSB’s Introduction supplies mutual superimposition; its 1.1.4 supplies Shankara’s own rope–snake comparison with liberating knowledge. Ordinary correction identifies the rope in both traditions; the philosophical extension of corrected error is what differs in §5.3. BG 3.8 concerns prescribed action and bodily maintenance, while 3.19 supplies the explicit instruction to act without attachment. BG 3.17–3.18 distinguishes the realised knower’s freedom from personal obligation, and 3.25–3.26 permits action for others’ guidance. The continued significance of empirical conduct does not reinstate obligatory individual doership after knowledge. BSB 2.1.13–2.1.14 preserves empirical distinctions while denying objects’ independent reality. The limits concerning usefulness, labour, and price in §5.7 refer to the examined passages, not the entire Advaita tradition.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The scientific discussion separates reward prediction error from decision valuation, cross-cultural regularity from exceptionless moral agreement, association from causation, and proxy failure from a proof of irreducible plurality. The 2010 income finding is read with the 2021 study and 2023 reanalysis. The critical questions concern the passages and proposals examined here; they do not assert that the wider Madhyasth Darshan literature contains no further treatment of education, constitution, economics, or institutional practice.
